criteria.name: Accurate
criteria.description: Every claim is either supported by the bill text or is accurate real-world context about the bill's subject (verifiable via general knowledge / web search). Nothing contradicts the bill text or the factual record.

criteria.name: No hallucinations
criteria.description: No fabricated or incorrect claims. Accurate context not stated in the bill — e.g. a program's common name, its administering agency, or the statute being amended — is acceptable and is NOT a hallucination. Only false or invented claims fail this criterion.

criteria.name: States purpose
criteria.description: The summary clearly identifies the bill's primary purpose or subject.

criteria.name: Changes to existing law
criteria.description: The summary describes how the bill amends, repeals, or adds to existing law (e.g. names the statute/program affected), when the bill does so.

criteria.name: Exceptions & conditions
criteria.description: The summary notes key exceptions, conditions, eligibility limits, or carve-outs that are material to the bill.

criteria.name: Effective dates & timing
criteria.description: The summary notes effective dates, sunsets, deadlines, or other timing provisions that the bill specifies.

criteria.name: Major provisions covered
criteria.description: Captures the bill's essential operative effect. A faithful high-level summary is fine; this fails only if a major operative provision is missing or misrepresented — not merely for omitting granular figures or minor sub-provisions.

criteria.name: Objective tone
criteria.description: The summary is neutral and non-partisan, with no advocacy, praise, criticism, or editorializing.

criteria.name: Coherent
criteria.description: The summary is well-organized, internally consistent, and reads clearly.

criteria.name: Concise
criteria.description: The summary avoids padding, repetition, boilerplate, and filler.

criteria.name: Correct entities
criteria.description: Any agencies, officials, programs, or statutes named — including accurate context beyond the bill text — are identified correctly. Adding a correct administering agency or program name is good; naming the wrong one fails.

criteria.name: Correct figures
criteria.description: Any dollar amounts, dates, or quantities the summary states are correct. Omitting figures does not fail this criterion; misstating one does.

expert.summary:
This joint resolution (H.J. Res. 20), enacted as Public Law 119-6, effects a congressional disapproval under the Congressional Review Act (chapter 8 of title 5, U.S. Code, specifically the mechanism established at 5 U.S.C. § 802) of a final rule promulgated by the Department of Energy.

The operative mechanism is the CRA's expedited disapproval procedure, whereby Congress, through a joint resolution presented to and signed by the President, nullifies a covered agency rule. The single operative clause provides that Congress disapproves the identified rule and that "such rule shall have no force or effect."

The targeted rule is the Department of Energy's "Energy Conservation Program: Energy Conservation Standards for Consumer Gas-fired Instantaneous Water Heaters," published at 89 Fed. Reg. 105188 (December 26, 2024). This rule was issued under DOE's authority to prescribe energy conservation standards for consumer products under the Energy Policy and Conservation Act.

The legal consequence of enactment is twofold and follows automatically from the CRA framework (5 U.S.C. § 801): first, the disapproved rule is deprived of legal effect and is treated as though it had never taken effect; second, by operation of 5 U.S.C. § 801(b)(2), the agency is barred from reissuing the rule in substantially the same form, or issuing a new rule that is substantially the same, absent subsequent statutory authorization enacted after the date of the disapproval resolution. The resolution itself contains no express language restating this reissuance bar; that limitation arises from the operation of the underlying CRA statute rather than from the text of the resolution.

The resolution contains no appropriation, no authorization of appropriations, no delegation of new rulemaking authority, no sunset provision, and no severability clause. It effects no amendment to the U.S. Code; its effect is limited to nullifying the specified agency rule.

The measure was considered and passed by the House on February 27, 2025, and considered and passed by the Senate on April 9 and 10, 2025 (the companion measure being S.J. Res. 4). It was approved by the President on May 9, 2025. As an enacted disapproval resolution, it takes effect upon approval; no deferred effective date or condition precedent is specified in the text.

This joint resolution, enacted as Public Law 119-5, exercises Congress's authority under the Congressional Review Act (chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code) to disapprove and nullify a final rule promulgated by the Internal Revenue Service.

The operative mechanism is the CRA's expedited disapproval procedure codified at 5 U.S.C. § 802. The resolution provides that Congress disapproves the IRS rule titled "Gross Proceeds Reporting by Brokers That Regularly Provide Services Effectuating Digital Asset Sales," published at 89 Fed. Reg. 106928 (December 30, 2024), and declares that "such rule shall have no force or effect." Upon the President's approval on April 10, 2025, the targeted rule is voided in its entirety.

Two substantive legal consequences flow from enactment under the CRA framework, though neither is restated in the resolution's text. First, under 5 U.S.C. § 801(b)(1), a rule disapproved by enacted joint resolution is treated as though it had never taken effect. Second, under 5 U.S.C. § 801(b)(2), the issuing agency may not reissue the rule in substantially the same form, nor issue a new rule that is substantially the same, absent subsequent statutory authorization. The resolution itself contains no express reference to these provisions, no amendment to the Internal Revenue Code, no savings clause, and no severability or effective-date language beyond the date of approval.

The disapproved rule concerns information-reporting obligations for so-called decentralized finance ("DeFi") brokers—persons who regularly provide services effectuating transfers of digital assets—including gross proceeds reporting requirements. Its nullification eliminates the reporting regime the IRS had established in that rulemaking.

The resolution effects no appropriation and confers no new regulatory authority; its sole legal effect is the negation of the identified agency rule. Its legislative history reflects passage of H.J. Res. 25 by the House on March 11, 2025, and by the Senate on March 26, 2025, with a companion measure (S.J. Res. 3) and a report from the House Committee on Ways and Means (H. Rept. 119-7).

This joint resolution, enacted as Public Law 119-2, exercises Congress's authority under the Congressional Review Act (CRA), codified at chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code (specifically 5 U.S.C. § 802), to disapprove and nullify a final rule promulgated by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).

The operative provision expresses congressional disapproval of the EPA rule titled "Waste Emissions Charge for Petroleum and Natural Gas Systems: Procedures for Facilitating Compliance, Including Netting and Exemptions," published at 89 Fed. Reg. 91094 (November 18, 2024). Pursuant to the resolution and the CRA mechanism, the resolution provides that "such rule shall have no force or effect."

The legal effect of enactment follows from 5 U.S.C. § 801(b) and (f): the disapproved rule is deprived of legal effect and is treated as though it had never taken effect. Additionally, under 5 U.S.C. § 801(b)(2), a rule that does not take effect (or is not continued in effect) by reason of a joint resolution of disapproval may not be reissued in substantially the same form, and a new rule that is substantially the same as the disapproved rule may not be issued, unless the reissued or new rule is specifically authorized by a law enacted after the date of the joint resolution of disapproval. The resolution itself does not recite this reissuance bar; it arises by operation of the underlying CRA statute.

The resolution contains no amendment to the United States Code, no authorization or appropriation of funds, no sunset provision, and no conditions precedent beyond enactment. It is a freestanding measure of disapproval whose sole operative function is nullification of the identified agency rule.

The legislative history reflects that H.J. Res. 35 was considered and passed by the House on February 26, 2025, and considered and passed by the Senate on February 27, 2025. A companion measure, S.J. Res. 12, is noted. The resolution was approved March 14, 2025. Because CRA joint resolutions are subject to presentment, approval on that date reflects presidential signature; the disapproval takes effect upon enactment. The bill specifies no separate effective date, deadline, or delayed applicability provision.

This measure is a request rather than a mandate; it expresses Congress's wishes but does not by its terms compel the Secretary to act or create new legal authority. expert.summary:
Public Law 119-46 (H.J. Res. 133) is a joint resolution requesting the Secretary of the Interior to authorize specific, temporary displays on the National Mall and the Washington Monument to initiate the commemoration of the United States Semiquincentennial. 

The resolution's operative mechanism consists of two formal requests by Congress. First, it requests the Secretary of the Interior to authorize unique and one-time arrangements for the display of United States semiquincentennial materials and other significant artifacts, digital content, film footage, and associated audio and imagery in and around the vicinity of the National Mall. This authorization includes projecting such content onto the surface of the Washington Monument for five nights of public display. The authorization is strictly time-limited, applying only during the period beginning on December 31, 2025, and ending on January 5, 2026. 

Second, the resolution respectfully requests that the Clerk of the House of Representatives transmit an enrolled copy of the resolution to the Secretary of the Interior and the Chair of the United States Semiquincentennial Commission.

The resolution includes a preamble citing historical precedents, including the United States Semiquincentennial Commission Act of 2016 (Public Law 114-196; 36 U.S.C. note prec. 101), which established the commission to plan the 250th-anniversary commemoration. It also references the 1976 Bicentennial and the 2019 Apollo 11 commemoration on the National Mall as precedents for lighting and projecting imagery on the Washington Monument.

The joint resolution does not amend existing provisions of the United States Code, nor does it provide any new permanent authority, appropriations, or regulatory mandates. It operates solely as a formal congressional request to an executive branch official and a directive to a House officer. The resolution was approved on December 2, 2025.

This bill is about stopping a special government order.

First, here is some background. A "national emergency" is when the President says there is a big problem that needs quick action. On July 30, 2025, the President declared a national emergency. That order added extra taxes, called "duties," on things brought into the United States from Brazil. These duties are also known as tariffs. They make goods from another country cost more.

This bill would end that emergency. If it becomes law, the emergency the President declared would be over. That means the special order about taxing goods from Brazil would stop.

The bill uses a rule from a law called the National Emergencies Act. This law lets Congress vote to end an emergency that a President started.

The bill was introduced in the House of Representatives on February 2, 2026. It was brought forward by Mr. Meeks and several other lawmakers. It was sent to a group called the Committee on Foreign Affairs. This group studies bills about how the United States deals with other countries.

The bill is short. It does one main thing: it ends the emergency from July 30, 2025.

expert.summary:
This joint resolution, introduced in the House as H.J. Res. 147 during the 119th Congress, 2d Session, invokes the congressional termination mechanism under section 202 of the National Emergencies Act (50 U.S.C. 1622) to terminate a specified presidential national emergency declaration.

The single operative provision terminates the national emergency declared by the President on July 30, 2025, in Executive Order 14323 (90 Fed. Reg. 37739). Per the resolution's caption and stated subject, that emergency provided the predicate for the imposition of duties on articles imported from Brazil.

The resolution proceeds under 50 U.S.C. 1622, which establishes the statutory procedure by which a national emergency may be terminated by enactment of a joint resolution. Consistent with that framework and the *INS v. Chadha*-driven 1985 amendments to the National Emergencies Act, termination by this route requires passage by both chambers and presentment to the President (subject to the possibility of veto and override), rather than a simple concurrent resolution.

The resolution contains no additional substantive provisions. It does not amend the Tariff Act, the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, or any other underlying trade or emergency-powers authority; it does not expressly address the disposition of duties already collected, nor does it specify an effective date, transition rules, or savings provisions. It contains no authorization of appropriations and effects no appropriation. Its legal effect is confined to terminating the identified emergency declaration, with any consequent cessation of duty authority flowing derivatively from that termination and the terms of the underlying Executive order.

The measure was referred to the House Committee on Foreign Affairs.

anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.label: anthropic/claude-opus-4.8
anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.summary:
This joint resolution, introduced in the House of Representatives in the 119th Congress, directs the President to remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities within or against the Republic of Cuba that Congress has not authorized.

The resolution begins with findings stating that the Constitution gives Congress the sole power to declare war, while the President has a responsibility to defend the United States and its citizens, service members, and diplomats from attack. It notes that Congress has not declared war on Cuba or enacted any specific statutory authorization for the use of military force within or against Cuba. The findings characterize the use of force against Cuba—including using the Coast Guard and other Armed Forces components to conduct a blockade or quarantine—as introducing U.S. Armed Forces into hostilities under section 4(a) of the War Powers Resolution.

The operative provision directs the President to remove U.S. Armed Forces from hostilities within or against Cuba, unless such action is explicitly authorized by a declaration of war or a specific authorization for use of military force. This directive is invoked under section 1013 of the Department of State Authorization Act, Fiscal Years 1984 and 1985, and is to be considered under the expedited procedures of section 601(b) of the International Security Assistance and Arms Export Control Act of 1976.

anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.summary:
The Investing in All of America Act of 2025 (Public Law 119-92) amends the Small Business Investment Act of 1958 to change the rules governing leverage available to Small Business Investment Companies (SBICs)—privately owned investment firms licensed by the Small Business Administration (SBA).

The bill revises the definition of "private capital" in the Act. It removes a requirement that certain qualifying institutional investments be "established prior to October 1, 1987," and expands eligible sources to include foundations, endowments, or trusts of colleges or universities. It also clarifies that private capital does not include funds obtained directly or indirectly from federal, state, or local governments (with limited exceptions) when the Administrator considers leverage requests.

The bill restructures the maximum leverage limits for SBICs. For a single company, it lowers one baseline leverage cap from $300 million to $200 million, and sets new caps of $250 million for companies making quarterly or semiannual interest payments and $175 million for other companies licensed under section 301(c). For companies under common control, it replaces the prior $350 million limit with $475 million for those making quarterly or semiannual interest payments and $350 million for others.

The bill broadens an exclusion from leverage calculations for investments in certain businesses. Previously focused on low-income geographic areas, the exclusion now also covers small business concerns in rural areas, businesses operating primarily in a "covered technology category" (as defined in title 10), and small manufacturers. The aggregate amount that may be excluded for a company or commonly controlled companies is capped at the lesser of 50 percent of their private capital or $125 million.

The exclusion applies only prospectively: an investment qualifies only if made after the date of enactment of the relevant provision.

The Act was approved on May 19, 2026.

anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.label: anthropic/claude-opus-4.8
anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.summary:
The "Stop Disaster Price Gouging Act" (H.R. 2427) would prohibit price gouging during federally declared major disasters or emergencies and classify such conduct as an unfair and deceptive act or practice.

After the President declares a major disaster or emergency under sections 401 or 501 of the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act, and within the declared area, the bill bars a person from raising prices more than 10 percent above the price charged the day before the declaration. This limit applies for 30 days to essential consumer goods and services, hotel lodging, and residential rentals, and for 180 days to repair or reconstruction services. It also bars charging a price more than 50 percent above the seller's cost for 30 days if that price was not charged before the declaration.

Exceptions apply when an increase is directly attributable to higher supplier, labor, or material costs (capped at 10 percent above cost plus the seller's customary markup), or to tariffs or national trade policies. Exceptions also cover regularly scheduled seasonal hotel/motel rate adjustments and rent increases tied to non-routine repairs or contractually agreed terms predating the disaster.

The bill defines "essential consumer goods and services" to include food, emergency and medical supplies, heating oil, construction materials, transportation, freight, storage, and fuel.

Enforcement: Violations are treated as violations of a Federal Trade Commission Act rule on unfair or deceptive practices, enforceable by the FTC. State attorneys general may sue on behalf of residents, with notice to the FTC, which may intervene; states cannot proceed against defendants named in a pending federal action. Injured individuals may bring private suits for injunctions and actual damages, with up to triple damages for willful violations, plus costs and attorney's fees, within two years of discovery.

Civil penalties are up to $25,000 per violation, with total liability for related acts capped at $25,000, adjusted annually for inflation. Recovered amounts fund affected disaster communities. The Act does not preempt non-conflicting state laws.

This bill is called the "Stop Disaster Price Gouging Act." It tries to stop stores and businesses from charging way too much for things after a big disaster or emergency.

Here is how it works. The President can declare a "major disaster or emergency" when something bad happens, like a big storm or flood. After that, businesses in that area must follow rules.

For important things people need — like food, water, medicine, gas, lumber, hotels, and rent — a business cannot raise the price more than 10 percent for 30 days. For fixing and rebuilding things, they cannot raise prices more than 10 percent for 180 days. Businesses also cannot charge a price that is more than 50 percent above what the item costs them.

There are some exceptions. If a business had to pay more to get the goods, or if new taxes on trade (called tariffs) raised the cost, higher prices may be allowed.

The Federal Trade Commission, a government group that watches over fair business, would enforce these rules. States and hurt people can also go to court. Businesses that break the rules can be fined up to $25,000. This amount can grow over time to keep up with rising prices.

The money collected from fines would go into a fund to help communities hit by disasters. People have up to 2 years to bring a case to court.

expert.summary:
The "Stop Disaster Price Gouging Act" (H.R. 2427, 119th Congress) would create a federal prohibition on price gouging during declared major disasters or emergencies, enforceable as an unfair or deceptive act or practice. The bill operates as freestanding law rather than by amending an existing act, though it incorporates enforcement machinery by reference.

**Prohibition (Section 2(a)).** Following a Presidential declaration under section 401 or 501 of the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act (42 U.S.C. 5170, 5191), and within the declared area, a person may not (i) increase the price of essential consumer goods and services, hotel lodging, and residential rental properties by more than 10 percent above the price the day before declaration, for 30 days; (ii) increase the price of repair or reconstruction services by more than 10 percent, for 180 days; and (iii) charge a price more than 50 percent above the person's cost for such goods/services for 30 days if not previously charging that price. Exceptions apply where the increase is directly attributable to increased supplier/labor/materials costs (subject to a customary-markup cap), attributable to tariffs or national trade policies, attributable to regularly scheduled seasonal hotel/motel adjustments, or attributable to amortized repair costs or pre-disaster contractual rent increases.

**FTC enforcement (Section 2(b)).** A violation is treated as a violation of a rule under section 18(a)(1)(B) of the FTC Act (15 U.S.C. 57a(a)(1)(B)) concerning unfair or deceptive acts or practices, enforceable by the Commission with the full powers and jurisdiction of the FTC Act (15 U.S.C. 41 et seq.).

**State enforcement (Section 2(c)).** State attorneys general or officials/agencies may bring parens patriae civil actions in state or federal court for injunctive relief, compliance, damages, restitution, or other relief, subject to prior written notice to the Commission, the Commission's intervention rights, and a stay-type limitation during a pending federal action.

**Private right of action (Section 2(d)).** Injured persons may sue for injunctive relief and actual monetary damages; courts may treble damages for willful violations, and shall award costs and reasonable attorney's fees to prevailing plaintiffs. A two-year discovery-based limitations period applies. The remedy is nonexclusive.

**Civil penalties (Section 2(e)).** Penalties are up to $25,000 per violation (each treated separately), but total liability for related acts may not exceed $25,000, with annual CPI adjustment beginning at least one year after enactment. Recovered amounts are deposited into a fund to assist affected communities.

**Definitions and preemption.** Section 2(f) enumerates "essential consumer goods and services." Section 2(g) provides that the Act does not preempt non-conflicting state law. No appropriation is made. No effective date beyond enactment is specified.

expert.summary:
H.R. 2427, the “Stop Disaster Price Gouging Act,” establishes a federal prohibition on price gouging during presidentially declared major disasters or emergencies. 

**Operative Prohibitions and Exceptions**
Section 2(a)(1) prohibits any person, within an area subject to a major disaster or emergency declaration under section 401 or 501 of the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act (42 U.S.C. §§ 5170, 5191), from increasing prices relative to the day preceding the declaration by more than 10 percent. This restriction applies to essential consumer goods and services, hotel lodging, and residential rental properties for 30 days, and to repair or reconstruction services for 180 days. Additionally, Section 2(a)(1)(B) prohibits charging a price more than 50 percent greater than the seller's cost for 30 days post-declaration if the seller did not charge that price prior to the declaration. 

Section 2(a)(2) provides affirmative exceptions if the price increase is directly attributable to:
*   Additional supplier, labor, or material costs, provided the price does not exceed 10 percent of the total cost plus the seller's customary pre-disaster markup;
*   Tariffs or national trade policies;
*   Regularly scheduled seasonal adjustments for hotel or motel rates; or
*   Amortized costs for non-maintenance rental repairs/additions, or pre-existing contractual agreements.

**Enforcement Mechanisms**
*   **Federal Trade Commission (FTC) Enforcement:** Section 2(b) designates violations as unfair or deceptive acts or practices under section 18(a)(1)(B) of the FTC Act (15 U.S.C. § 57a(a)(1)(B)). The FTC is granted standard enforcement powers, jurisdiction, and duties under the FTC Act (15 U.S.C. § 41 et seq.).
*   **State Enforcement:** Section 2(c) authorizes state attorneys general or designated state officials to bring civil actions *parens patriae* in state or federal district courts to enjoin violations, compel compliance, or seek damages and restitution. States must provide prior or immediate written notice and a copy of the complaint to the FTC. The FTC retains the right to intervene and appeal. State actions are barred during the pendency of a parallel federal civil action against the same defendant.
*   **Private Right of Action:** Section 2(d) establishes a private right of action in state or federal district court for injunctive relief and actual damages. Courts may award treble damages for willful violations, as well as costs and reasonable attorney's fees. The statute of limitations is two years from discovery or reasonable opportunity of discovery.

**Penalties and Funding**
Section 2(e) establishes civil penalties of up to $25,000 per violation, subject to a maximum aggregate liability of $25,000 for related violations. These caps are subject to annual inflation adjustments based on the Consumer Price Index, beginning at least one year post-enactment. Civil penalties recovered by the FTC must be deposited into a fund to assist communities in Stafford Act disaster zones.

**Preemption**
Section 2(g) preserves state laws except to the extent that they directly conflict with the Act.

Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act (42 U.S.C. 5170, 5191). The prohibition is subject to specific exceptions: an increase is permitted if it is directly attributable to additional supplier, labor, or materials costs and does not exceed the cost plus the seller’s customary pre-disaster markup by more than 10 percent; if it is directly attributable to tariffs or national trade policies; for hotel or motel rates, if attributable to regularly scheduled seasonal adjustments; or for rental rates, if attributable to amortized repair or addition costs beyond normal maintenance or if the increase was contractually agreed to by the tenant prior to the disaster or emergency.

A violation of the prohibition is treated as a violation of a rule under section 18(a)(1)(B) of the Federal Trade Commission Act (15 U.S.C. 57a(a)(1)(B)) regarding unfair or deceptive acts or practices. The FTC shall enforce the prohibition using all powers and procedures of the FTC Act (15 U.S.C. 41 et seq.). Civil penalties are calculated per violation at up to $25,000, but the total liability for all violations resulting from the same or related acts or practices is capped at $25,000. The penalty amounts are subject to annual inflation adjustments based on the Consumer Price Index beginning one year after enactment. Amounts recovered by the FTC are deposited into a fund to assist communities in disaster-affected areas.

State attorneys general (or designated officials) may bring civil actions as parens patriae in state or federal court for injunctive relief, compliance, damages, restitution, or other equitable relief. Prior notice to the FTC is required; the FTC may intervene, be heard, and petition for appeal. State actions are barred during the pendency of a federal action by the FTC or the U.S. Attorney General against the same defendant for the same alleged violation. The bill does not limit States’ own investigative powers.

A private right of action is created: an injured person may sue in state or federal court for injunctive relief, actual monetary damages, or both. For willful violations, the court may award treble damages. A prevailing plaintiff is entitled to costs and reasonable attorney’s fees. Actions must be commenced within two years of discovery or reasonable opportunity to discover the violation. The private remedy is nonexclusive.

The bill defines “essential consumer goods and services” as goods and services necessary for survival and recovery, enumerating categories including food and drink, emergency supplies, medical supplies, home heating oil, building materials, transportation, freight, storage, and motor fuels. anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.label: anthropic/claude-opus-4.8
anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.summary:
The "No Visas for Anti-Semitic Students Act" (H.R. 2866) directs the Secretary of State to revoke or deny student visas to foreign nationals who engage in antisemitic conduct.

Under Section 2, the Secretary of State must revoke or deny a visa issued under subparagraph (F) or (M) of section 101(a)(15) of the Immigration and Nationality Act—categories covering academic and vocational students—for any alien who, on or after the bill's enactment date, both (1) engages in "prohibited antisemitic conduct" and (2) is determined by the Secretary to pose potentially serious adverse foreign policy consequences for the United States under section 237(a)(4)(C)(i) of the Act.

The bill defines "antisemitism" using the definition adopted by the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance on May 26, 2016, as adopted by the State Department, including its "contemporary examples of antisemitism." It defines "prohibited antisemitic conduct" as either (A) committing a physical act of violence, vandalism, or harassment targeting a Jewish individual, their property, a community institution, or a religious facility, with intent to intimidate or harm based on Jewish identity or affiliation; or (B) providing material support—including funding, organizing, or inciting—to a person knowing they intended to use it to commit such an act.

Section 3 amends section 214 of the Immigration and Nationality Act by adding a new subsection (s). This provision states that an alien may not be granted or maintain (F) or (M) nonimmigrant status if the alien engages in prohibited antisemitic conduct and the Secretary determines such conduct would have potentially serious adverse foreign policy consequences. It further requires the Secretary to revoke the visa of an alien already holding such status upon making these determinations. The new subsection incorporates the same definitions of "antisemitism" and "prohibited antisemitic conduct."

The bill's provisions apply to conduct occurring on or after the date of enactment. It was introduced on April 10, 2025, and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

expert.summary:
H.R. 2866, the "No Visas for Anti-Semitic Students Act," introduced in the 119th Congress (1st Session) by Ms. Malliotakis and referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary, directs the Secretary of State to revoke or deny student visas to aliens determined to have engaged in antisemitic conduct.

Section 2(a) mandates that the Secretary of State revoke or deny a visa under subparagraph (F) (academic students) or (M) (vocational students) of section 101(a)(15) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) (8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(15)) to any alien who, on or after the date of enactment, both (1) engages in "prohibited antisemitic conduct" and (2) is determined by the Secretary, pursuant to INA § 237(a)(4)(C)(i) (8 U.S.C. 1227(a)(4)(C)(i)) (the foreign-policy deportability ground), to pose potentially serious adverse foreign policy consequences for the United States through such conduct. Both conditions are prerequisites, and the provision applies prospectively (conduct occurring on or after enactment).

Section 2(b) defines "antisemitism" by reference to the definition adopted May 26, 2016, by the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA), as adopted by the Department of State, including its "contemporary examples of antisemitism." "Prohibited antisemitic conduct" is defined as (A) engaging in a physical act of violence, vandalism, or harassment targeting a Jewish individual, their property, a community institution, or religious facility, with intent to intimidate or harm based on Jewish identity or affiliation; or (B) providing material support (including funding, organizing, or inciting) to a person knowing that the person intended to use such support to engage in conduct described in subparagraph (A).

Section 3 amends INA § 214 (8 U.S.C. 1184) by adding a new subsection (s). Paragraph (s)(1) bars an alien from being granted or maintaining F or M nonimmigrant status where the alien engages in prohibited antisemitic conduct and the Secretary makes the § 237(a)(4)(C)(i) foreign-policy determination. Paragraph (s)(2) requires the Secretary to revoke the visa of an alien already in F or M status upon determining that the alien engaged in prohibited antisemitic conduct and that the alien or conduct poses potentially serious adverse foreign policy consequences. Paragraph (s)(3) incorporates definitions parallel to those in Section 2(b).

The bill contains no separate effective-date provision (taking effect upon enactment), no authorization of appropriations, and no sunset. The operative revocation/denial obligations are cast as mandatory ("shall").

anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.summary:
The Safer Response Act of 2025 (H.R. 4079) amends Section 546 of the Public Health Service Act to reauthorize and modify a federal grant program that supports the training of first responders and the provision of overdose-reversal drugs.

The bill makes several substantive changes to the existing program. First, it broadens the type of drugs covered by the program. Where current law refers to drugs "approved or cleared" by the Food and Drug Administration, the bill replaces this phrase throughout with "approved, cleared, or otherwise legally marketed," potentially expanding the categories of qualifying overdose-reversal drugs.

Second, the bill expands the program's scope beyond opioids. It removes the word "opioid" in multiple places, so that the grants and related training apply to drug overdoses generally rather than only opioid-related overdoses. Specifically, in the provision describing covered training, language referring to "opioid and heroin" overdoses is changed to "opioid, heroin, and other drug" overdoses, and references to "opioid overdose" are changed to "overdose."

Third, the bill reauthorizes funding for the program. It strikes the prior authorization of $36,000,000 for each of fiscal years 2019 through 2023 and replaces it with an authorization of $57,000,000 for each of fiscal years 2026 through 2030.

The bill also makes a technical change, capitalizing "Tribes and Tribal" where those terms appear in subsection (a).

The legislation was introduced in the House of Representatives on June 23, 2025, and referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce.

The operative amendments are as follows:

First, in subsection (a), the bill makes a conforming capitalization change, striking "tribes and tribal" and inserting "Tribes and Tribal."

Second, throughout subsections (a), (c), and (d), the bill broadens the category of covered products by striking "approved or cleared" wherever it appears and inserting "approved, cleared, or otherwise legally marketed"—thereby encompassing products lawfully marketed through pathways other than FDA approval or clearance. Third, subsection (f) is amended in parallel fashion. The "approved, cleared, or otherwise legally marketed" language is substituted for "approved or cleared" wherever it appears. Fourth, subsection (h) revises the authorization of appropriations. The bill strikes the prior authorization of "$36,000,000 for each of fiscal years 2019 through 2023" and inserts "$57,000,000 for each of fiscal years 2026 through 2030." This bill is called the Safer Response Act of 2025. It keeps a government program going that gives money to train first responders like police, firefighters, and paramedics. The training teaches them how to help someone who has taken too much of a drug (an overdose).

The bill makes a few changes. Before, the training only covered overdoses from a certain kind of drug called opioids. Now it covers overdoses from any drug, including heroin and others. It also allows trainers to teach about more medicines that can reverse an overdose, as long as those medicines are legally sold.

Another change is about money. The program used to provide $36 million each year. The bill raises that amount to $57 million each year. It also sets new dates for the program to run from 2026 through 2030. Finally, the bill fixes a small writing mistake by capitalizing the word “Tribes.”

If the bill becomes law, first responders will have broader training and more funding to help save lives in overdose emergencies.

The "Securing Community Upgrades for a Resilient Grid Act" or "SECURE Grid Act" (H.R. 7257) amends Section 366 of the Energy Policy and Conservation Act to require States to address the physical security, cybersecurity, and resilience of local electricity distribution systems within their State energy security plans.

The bill defines a "local distribution system" as energy infrastructure owned and operated by an electric utility at 100 kilovolts or less. It expands the consultation requirement so that States coordinate not only with owners and operators of energy infrastructure but also with suppliers of equipment for generating, transmitting, and distributing electricity.

The bill revises the content requirements for State plans. Plans must address physical threats and vulnerabilities (including weather-related threats, physical attacks on local distribution and bulk-power systems, and supply-chain risks for electricity equipment) and cybersecurity threats and vulnerabilities (including threats to local distribution systems that may affect the bulk-power system). Plans must also provide a risk-mitigation approach for responding to, mitigating, and recovering from such hazards.

The legislation clarifies that, while a State must submit a plan to be eligible for certain assistance, the submission does not require Secretary of Energy approval. It changes the provision governing federal technical assistance from discretionary ("may") to mandatory ("shall"). It also extends information-protection provisions to cover local distribution systems and sets a new sunset date of September 30, 2031, for Section 366.

Section 3 directs the Comptroller General (GAO) to submit a report by September 30, 2030, to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee. The report must evaluate the effectiveness of State energy security plans, offer recommendations for improving State capabilities and federal coordination, and provide information on federal financial assistance used to implement plans and related State activities. The report must be publicly available, except that information protected under Section 366(h) must be placed in a non-public annex.

As reported by the Committee on Energy and Commerce, the text was amended by striking all language after the enacting clause and inserting new text.

The power grid is how electricity travels to homes and buildings. This bill focuses on the "local distribution system." That means the smaller power equipment near people's homes, using lower amounts of electricity. Bigger power lines are not part of this.

The bill changes a law about "State energy security plans." These are plans that each state makes to keep energy safe. The bill says states must now think about more dangers in their plans. These dangers include:

The bill as reported reflects a Committee on Energy and Commerce amendment in the nature of a substitute (striking all after the enacting clause).

Section 2 makes the following amendments to 42 U.S.C. 6326:

- Subsection (a) is amended to add a new paragraph (3) defining "local distribution system" as energy infrastructure owned and operated by an electric utility at 100 kilovolts or less.
- Subsection (b)(2) is amended to add suppliers of equipment for the generation, transmission, and distribution of electricity to the list of consulted entities.
- Subsection (c) is amended by replacing paragraph (3) to require plans to address enumerated physical threats (weather-related, physical attacks on local distribution and bulk-power systems, and supply chain risks) and cybersecurity threats (including threats to local distribution systems that may impact the bulk-power system), and by replacing paragraph (5) to require a risk mitigation approach for end-use resilience, including response, mitigation, and recovery methods.
- Subsection (d)(3) is amended to add a new subparagraph (B) addressing equipment supply, redesignating the prior subparagraph (B) as (C).
- Subsection (e) is restructured; existing text becomes paragraph (1) ("Submission required"), and a new paragraph (2) ("State determination") specifies that a submission is not required to be approved by the Secretary.
- Subsection (f) is amended by striking "may" and inserting "shall," converting discretionary Secretarial assistance to a mandatory obligation.
- Subsection (h) is amended to extend its protected-information provisions to local distribution systems.
- Subsection (i) is replaced with a sunset causing Section 366 to expire on September 30, 2031.

Section 3 directs the Comptroller General, not later than September 30, 2030, to submit a report to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources on the efficacy of State energy security plans. The report must include an evaluation of plans' effect on States' risk identification and recovery capabilities; recommendations for improvement and enhanced Secretary–State coordination; information on federal financial assistance under EPCA part D of title III (42 U.S.C. 6321 et seq.) and associated State activities; an analysis of the implementation of amended Section 366; and information on State use of assistance under amended Section 366(f), including resulting plan revisions. Under subsection (b), the report must be publicly releasable, except that information protected under Section 366(h) must be placed in a non-public annex. Subsection (c) incorporates the Section 366(a) definition of "State energy security plan."

The bill contains no appropriation.

The main goal is to make sure states plan to protect the local power lines that bring electricity to homes, schools, and businesses. These local lines are called “local distribution systems.” They carry electricity at lower voltages (100 kilovolts or less).

Right now, states must write energy security plans to get certain help from the federal government. This bill adds new rules for those plans. States would have to include ways to keep local power systems safe from physical dangers like bad weather, attacks, and problems getting equipment. They also must plan for cybersecurity threats, like computer attacks that could cause blackouts.

The bill says the U.S. Department of Energy must (not just may) give states money and support to create and update these plans. States do not need the Energy Secretary to approve their plan. They just need to have one. The bill also says companies that supply power equipment should be included in planning talks.

The new rules would end on September 30, 2031. By September 30, 2030, a government watchdog called the GAO must write a report. The report will check how well the state plans worked, how federal money was used, and suggest improvements. Some secret security details in the report would be kept private.

expert.summary:
The bill, cited as the “Securing Community Upgrades for a Resilient Grid Act” or the “SECURE Grid Act,” amends section 366 of the Energy Policy and Conservation Act (EPCA) (42 U.S.C. 6326) to require States to integrate the physical security, cybersecurity, and resilience of local distribution systems into their State energy security plans. The legislation does not appropriate funds; it primarily restructures and expands existing statutory planning requirements and assistance duties.

Section 2 amends EPCA section 366 in several respects. It adds a new definition in subsection (a)(3) for “local distribution system,” meaning energy infrastructure owned and operated by an electric utility at a voltage of 100 kilovolts or less. Subsection (b)(2) is revised to require that, in developing a State energy security plan, the State must consult not only owners and operators of energy infrastructure but also “suppliers of equipment for the generation, transmission, and distribution of electricity.” Subsection (c) is amended to rewrite plan-content elements: paragraph (3) now more granularly requires plans to address physical threats (weather-related threats, physical attacks on local distribution systems and the bulk-power system, and supply chain risks for generation, transmission, and distribution equipment) and cybersecurity threats and vulnerabilities, including threats to local distribution systems that may impact the bulk-power system. Paragraph (5) is revised to require a risk-mitigation approach that enhances reliability and end-use resilience, encompassing methods for responding to, mitigating, and recovering from the hazards described in paragraph (3).

Subsection (d)(3) is amended to insert a new subparagraph (B) that adds “supplying equipment for the generation, transmission, and distribution of electricity” to the entities covered by that provision; existing subparagraph (B) is redesignated as subparagraph (C). In subsection (e), the amendment restructures the text: it designates the existing eligibility condition as paragraph (1) (“Submission required”) and adds a new paragraph (2) (“State determination”) providing that a submission under paragraph (1) “is not required to be approved by the Secretary.” This eliminates the requirement for Secretarial approval of a State’s energy security plan as a condition of eligibility. Subsection (f) is amended by striking “may” and inserting “shall,” converting the Secretary’s authority to provide assistance to States from discretionary to mandatory. Subsection (h) is amended to extend its confidentiality protections to information relating to local distribution systems. Subsection (i) is struck and replaced with a new sunset provision: “This section shall expire on September 30, 2031.”

Section 3 directs the Comptroller General to submit a report to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources not later than September 30, 2030. The report must evaluate the efficacy of State energy security plans; make recommendations to improve State risk-identification and -mitigation and to enhance the Secretary of Energy’s coordination with States; provide data on federal financial assistance under part D of title III of EPCA (42 U.S.C. 6321 et seq.) used to implement the plans and on State activities funded therewith; analyze the efficacy of the implementation of the amended section 366; and detail State use of assistance under section 366(f) and any resulting plan revisions. Any information protected from disclosure under section 366(h) must be placed in a non-public annex. The term “State energy security plan” is defined by reference to section 366(a).

crs_reference.summary:
Securing Community Upgrades for a Resilient Grid Act or the SECURE Grid Act
This bill extends through FY2031 and modifies requirements for state energy security plans. Under current law, states are required to submit to the Department of Energy (DOE) state energy security plans that meet certain requirements in order to be eligible to receive federal financial assistance for state energy conservation programs. 
The bill specifies that DOE is not required to approve the plans. 
The bill requires DOE to provide information, technical assistance, and other assistance in the development, implementation, or revision of a state energy security plan upon the request of a state.
The bill also requires states to address additional factors in their energy security plans, such as (1) weather-related threats and vulnerabilities; (2) supply chain risks for equipment for the generation, transmission, and distribution of electricity; and (3) the security of local distribution systems and the bulk-power system. A local distribution system is energy infrastructure owned and operated by an electric utility at a voltage of 100 kilovolts or less.
In addition, the bill directs the Government Accountability Office to report to Congress on the efficacy of state energy security plans.

anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.summary:
The Energy Emergency Leadership Act (H.R. 7258) amends the Department of Energy Organization Act to formally assign energy emergency and energy security functions to an Assistant Secretary within the Department of Energy.

Specifically, the bill adds a new paragraph to Section 203(a) of the Act, designating responsibilities related to energy emergencies and security. These functions include responsibilities concerning energy infrastructure, security and resilience, emerging threats, cybersecurity, supply, and emergency planning, preparedness, coordination, response, and restoration. The provision also authorizes the Department, upon request from a State, local, or Tribal government or an energy sector entity, to provide technical assistance and support to protect against, detect, and respond to energy security threats, risks, and incidents. Such assistance is to be carried out in coordination with other federal agencies as appropriate.

The bill further directs the Secretary of Energy to ensure that these newly assigned functions are performed in coordination with relevant federal agencies.

The legislation does not specify an effective date or set deadlines, and it does not establish new funding. The bill was introduced in the House on January 27, 2026, referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, and subsequently ordered to be printed after being committed to the Committee of the Whole House.

expert.summary:
H.R. 7258, the "Energy Emergency Leadership Act," would amend section 203(a) of the Department of Energy Organization Act (42 U.S.C. 7133(a)) to expand the categories of functions the Secretary of Energy may assign to Assistant Secretaries. The bill's operative mechanism is the addition of a new paragraph (12) to that subsection, enumerating "[e]nergy emergency and energy security functions" as among the assignable functions.

New paragraph (12) specifies two components. Subparagraph (A) covers responsibilities relating to energy infrastructure, security and resilience, emerging threats, cybersecurity, supply, and emergency planning, preparedness, coordination, response, and restoration, each qualified by "as appropriate." Subparagraph (B) authorizes, upon request of a State, local, or Tribal government or an energy sector entity, and in coordination with other Federal agencies as appropriate, the provision of technical assistance and support to protect against, detect, and respond to energy security threats, risks, and incidents.

Section 2(b) imposes a coordination directive, requiring the Secretary of Energy to ensure that the functions described in the newly added section 203(a)(12) are performed in coordination with relevant Federal agencies.

The bill effects a structural and organizational amendment to the enumeration of Assistant Secretary functions; it does not itself assign the functions to a designated Assistant Secretary, create a new office or position, prescribe a definition of "energy sector entity," or establish deadlines, reporting requirements, or sunset provisions. It contains no authorization of appropriations and makes no appropriation. No effective date is specified, so the amendments would take effect upon enactment.

Procedurally, the bill was introduced January 27, 2026, by Ms. Lee of Florida and Mr. Walberg, referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, and on May 11, 2026, reported (Report No. 119-645) and committed to the Committee of the Whole House on the State of the Union.

The "Rural and Municipal Utility Cybersecurity Act" (H.R. 7266) amends Section 40124 of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act to reauthorize and revise the Rural and Municipal Utility Advanced Cybersecurity Grant and Technical Assistance Program, which is administered by the Secretary (of Energy).

The bill directs the Secretary to maintain this program, which provides technical assistance and funding—including grants, cooperative agreements, and prizes—to eligible electric utilities to help them protect against, detect, respond to, and recover from cybersecurity threats. The program's stated objectives are to deploy advanced cybersecurity technologies for electric utility systems and to increase participation of eligible entities in cybersecurity threat information-sharing programs.

The bill defines "eligible entity" to include rural electric cooperatives; electric utilities owned by political subdivisions of a State (such as municipally owned utilities); utilities owned by agencies, authorities, corporations, or instrumentalities of one or more political subdivisions; certain not-for-profit entities partnered with at least six such utilities; and investor-owned utilities selling less than 4,000,000 megawatt hours of electricity per year. It also defines terms such as "advanced cybersecurity technology," "bulk-power system," "cybersecurity threat," and "defense critical electric infrastructure" by reference to existing law.

In carrying out the program, the Secretary must (subject to available appropriations) provide assistance and funding on a competitive or noncompetitive basis, develop award criteria, and establish a process to inform eligible entities of opportunities. The Secretary may enter into agreements with eligible entities. Priority is to be given to entities that have limited cybersecurity resources, own assets critical to bulk-power system reliability, or own or operate defense critical electric infrastructure.

Information shared by or with federal, State, Tribal, or local governments under the program is deemed voluntarily shared and exempt from disclosure under the federal Freedom of Information Act and comparable State, Tribal, or local open-records laws.

The bill authorizes $250,000,000 in appropriations to the Secretary for fiscal years 2026 through 2030.

The "Energy Threat Analysis Center Act of 2026" (H.R. 7305) amends Section 40125(c) of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act to reauthorize and expand the Department of Energy's Energy Sector Operational Support for Cyberresilience Program, which provides operational support for cybersecurity and resilience in the U.S. energy sector.

The bill adds new purposes to the program aimed at strengthening the collective defense, response, and resilience of the energy sector. These include enhancing collaboration between the government and the energy sector to analyze and mitigate threats by exchanging classified and unclassified information, building technical infrastructure for advanced analytics and threat analysis, advancing understanding of national security risks and vulnerabilities that adversaries might exploit, and increasing knowledge of threat actor tactics, techniques, and indicators of compromise.

The bill authorizes the Secretary of Energy to carry out program activities through an Energy Threat Analysis Center, which may be established at one or more physical locations.

Several procedural provisions are added:
- The provision of assistance or information to any government or private entity is at the Secretary's sole and unreviewable discretion and creates no right or benefit (substantive or procedural) for other entities to receive similar assistance.
- The program is not subject to the Federal Advisory Committee Act (chapter 10 of title 5).
- Information shared with or by federal, state, tribal, or local governments under the program is deemed voluntarily shared and exempt from disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act and comparable state, tribal, or local disclosure laws, and must be withheld from the public.
- The Secretary is granted transaction authority to enter into contracts, cooperative agreements, grants, and other transactions with public agencies, private organizations, and persons, and may establish pre-approved national security contracting mechanisms, model partnership agreements, and expedited review procedures to minimize delays.

Finally, the bill updates the program's authorization of appropriations period from fiscal years 2022 through 2026 to fiscal years 2027 through 2031.

The bill was introduced February 2, 2026, and reported with an amendment on May 12, 2026.

anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.summary:
The Kids Internet and Digital Safety Act (KIDS Act) is a comprehensive bill aimed at protecting minors (defined as individuals under 17) online. It establishes new requirements across several categories of online services and provides for enforcement by the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and state attorneys general.

**Title I (SCREEN Act):** Within one year of enactment, websites where more than one-third of content is "sexual material harmful to minors" must adopt age-verification technology to prevent minors' access. The bill prohibits requiring users to submit government-issued ID and requires data-security protections.

**Title II:** This title applies to social media-type "covered platforms." Subtitle A (Kids Online Safety Act) requires platforms to adopt policies addressing harms to minors (e.g., sexual exploitation, sale of drugs/alcohol/gambling, financial deception); provide safeguards and parental tools (with default protective settings); offer reporting mechanisms with deadlines (10 days, or sooner for imminent threats); disclose advertising practices; and undergo annual third-party audits. Subtitle B (SMK Act) bans ephemeral messaging for minors and direct messaging for children under 13, and requires parental controls for teens' messaging. Subtitle C (SPY Kids Act) restricts market research on minors.

**Title III (Safer GAMING Act):** Online video game providers must give parents communication-limiting safeguards (enabled by default at the most protective level) and other controls.

**Title IV (SAFE BOTs Act):** AI chatbot providers must disclose that the chatbot is not human, provide crisis-hotline resources, suggest breaks after three hours, and avoid falsely claiming to be licensed professionals.

**Title V:** Requires multiple studies and reports (on social media use, fentanyl access, safety tools, and chatbots' mental-health effects), educational campaigns, and a Kids Internet Safety Partnership.

**Title VI:** Provides for FTC and state enforcement, channels constitutional challenges exclusively to the D.C. Circuit (with 90/60-day limits), and includes rules preserving encryption, Section 230, and COPPA.

Most provisions take effect one year after enactment, with exceptions (e.g., Subtitle B at 180 days, Subtitle C at 90 days). The bill preempts certain conflicting state laws while preserving others.

This bill is called the "Kids Internet and Digital Safety Act," or "KIDS Act." It tries to make the internet safer for kids under 17. Here are the big parts:

**Blocking bad content:** Websites where more than one-third of the content is sexual and harmful to kids must use technology to check if a user is a minor. They must block minors from seeing that content. This starts one year after the law passes. Kids won't have to show a government ID.

**Safety on apps and social media:** Big platforms must make tools to protect kids. Kids get the safest settings by default. Parents get tools to manage settings, limit screen time, and control spending. Platforms must let people report harm to a kid and answer within 10 days. They cannot advertise drugs, alcohol, tobacco, or gambling to kids.

**Safer messaging:** Kids under 13 can't use direct messaging on these platforms. Disappearing messages are banned for all minors. Teens (13–16) get parent controls for messaging.

**Video games:** Online games must give parents tools to limit who can talk to their kids.

**AI chatbots:** Chatbots must tell kids they are not real people. They must share a crisis hotline if a kid talks about suicide. They must tell kids to take a break after 3 hours.

**Studies and teaching:** The government will study social media, fentanyl sales, and chatbots, and teach families about online safety.

The Federal Trade Commission and states can enforce these rules.

expert.summary:
The "Kids Internet and Digital Safety Act" or "KIDS Act" (H.R. 7757, 119th Cong.) is an omnibus bill establishing federal requirements for online platforms, chatbots, and gaming services concerning minors (defined in § 2(8) as individuals under 17), enforced primarily by the FTC. It contains six titles.

**Title I ("SCREEN Act")** requires providers of "covered platforms"—platforms where more than one-third of material is "sexual material harmful to minors" knowingly made available—to adopt commercially available "technology verification measures" and prevent minor access, beginning one year post-enactment (§ 103). Providers may not require government-issued ID (§ 103(e)), must observe data-minimization and security standards, and the FTC must consult specified experts (§ 104). GAO must report within three years (§ 105). Section 106 preempts state laws imposing parallel verification mandates, subject to savings clauses for tort, contract, criminal, and consumer-protection laws.

**Title II** defines "covered platform" (§ 201) and contains four subtitles. **Subtitle A ("Kids Online Safety Act")** requires reasonable policies addressing enumerated harms without imposing a duty of care (§ 213(c)(2)), minor safeguards and parental tools with most-protective default settings (§ 214), reporting mechanisms with a 10-day response window (§ 215), disclosures and verifiable parental consent (§ 216), advertising labels (§ 217), a prohibition on advertising illegal products to minors (§ 218), and annual independent third-party audits with FTC and public reporting (§ 219). Section 220 disclaims any age-verification mandate; § 221 preempts conflicting state law. **Subtitle B ("SMK Act")** prohibits ephemeral messaging for minors (§ 233) and direct messaging for children under 13 (§ 234), and mandates parental direct-messaging controls for teens (§ 235), with an encryption savings clause (§ 236); effective 180 days post-enactment except § 235 (§ 238). **Subtitle C ("SPY Kids Act")** prohibits market/product research on minors subject to exceptions (§ 243); effective 90 days post-enactment (§ 245).

**Title III ("Safer GAMING Act")** requires online video game providers to supply default-enabled, most-protective communication safeguards and parental tools (§ 303).

**Title IV ("SAFE BOTs Act")** prohibits chatbots from falsely claiming professional licensure (§ 403), mandates AI-status and crisis-resource disclosures (§ 404), and requires break advisories after three hours and harm-mitigation policies (§ 405).

**Title V** mandates multiple studies and reports (FTC, HHS, NIH), and amends Subtitle A of the Protecting Children in the 21st Century Act (15 U.S.C. 6551 et seq.) by striking and replacing §§ 211–214, 216 to establish an FTC public-awareness campaign with ten years of annual reports (§ 522). It creates a Commerce-administered Kids Internet Safety Partnership that sunsets five years after establishment (§ 526).

**Title VI** provides FTC enforcement via FTC Act § 18(a)(1)(B) and state parens patriae actions (§ 601), vests exclusive constitutional-challenge jurisdiction in the D.C. Circuit with 90/60-day limitations (§ 602), includes First Amendment, Section 230, encryption, and COPPA savings clauses (§ 603), severability (§ 604), and a general one-year effective date (§ 605). The bill authorizes no appropriations.

The Kids Internet and Digital Safety Act would establish federal requirements intended to protect minors online, with enforcement by the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general.

The bill would require certain publicly accessible online platforms where more than one-third of content is sexual material harmful to minors to use commercially available age-verification or age-estimation technology, beginning one year after enactment, and to prevent minors from accessing that material. Self-attestation would not be sufficient, government identification could not be required, and verification data could not be retained or shared beyond what is strictly necessary.

For covered social-media-like platforms, the bill would require policies addressing specified harms to minors, including severe threats of violence, sexual exploitation and abuse, illegal or age-restricted products, and financial harms from deceptive practices. Platforms would have to provide default protective safeguards for known minors, parental tools, reporting mechanisms with timely responses, notices, advertising disclosures, and annual independent audits, with the first audit due within 18 months. The bill states these provisions do not require age gating or age verification.

The bill would prohibit covered platforms from offering ephemeral messaging to known minors and direct messaging to known users under 13, and would require parental direct-message controls for known teen users. These provisions generally take effect 180 days after enactment, except the teen parental-control section, which is subject to the Act’s general one-year effective date. The bill also prohibits certain market or product-focused research on known minors, with exceptions for safety-related purposes and legal compliance; that provision takes effect after 90 days.

The bill would require online video game providers to give parents default protective controls over communications, purchases, time limits, and profile recommendations for known minor users. Chatbot providers could not falsely state that a chatbot is a licensed professional, would have to disclose to known minors that the chatbot is AI, provide crisis hotline resources when suicide is raised, prompt breaks after three hours, and maintain policies addressing specified harmful content.

The bill also directs federal studies, reports, educational resources, and a temporary Kids Internet Safety Partnership, and amends the Protecting Children in the 21st Century Act to create an FTC-led internet safety education campaign. It includes state-law preemption provisions with exceptions, encryption protections, severability, and special rules for constitutional challenges.

The Kids Internet and Digital Safety Act (KIDS Act) establishes federal requirements for covered online services used by minors, enforced principally by the Federal Trade Commission as violations of rules under Federal Trade Commission Act § 18(a)(1)(B), 15 U.S.C. § 57a(a)(1)(B), with parens patriae civil enforcement by State attorneys general subject to FTC notice, intervention, and federal-action preclusion.

Title I, the SCREEN Act, requires, beginning 1 year after enactment, providers of publicly accessible platforms on which more than one-third of knowingly made-available material is “sexual material harmful to minors” to adopt commercially available technology verification measures, prevent minors from accessing such material, provide notice, address circumvention, minimize transfer/disclosure/retention of verification data, and maintain reasonable data security. It authorizes third-party verification without relieving provider liability, disclaims any requirement to submit government identification, requires FTC consultation, and directs a GAO report within 3 years. It preempts State age-verification requirements for such platforms, with savings clauses for specified State laws.

Title II defines covered platforms and imposes minors’ online-safety obligations. Subtitle A, the Kids Online Safety Act, requires reasonable policies addressing enumerated harms to minors; safeguards and default protective settings for known minors; parental tools, including defaults for known children; reporting mechanisms with substantive responses within 10 days or sooner for imminent threats; disclosures and parental-consent processes; advertising labels for paid endorsements; a prohibition on facilitating advertising of specified illegal or age-restricted products to known minors; and independent annual audits beginning 18 months after enactment with FTC and public reporting. It disclaims any age-gating or age-verification mandate and preempts conflicting State law. Subtitle B, the Safe Messaging for Kids Act, prohibits ephemeral messaging for known minors, prohibits direct messaging for known users under 13, and requires parental direct-messaging controls for known teen users, subject to encryption-preservation rules; it takes effect 180 days after enactment except § 235, which follows the Act’s default effective date. Subtitle C, the SPY Kids Act, effective 90 days after enactment, prohibits market or product-focused research on known minors except for safety/privacy-related improvement or legal compliance.

Title III, the Safer GAMING Act, requires online video game providers to furnish default, most-protective parental communication safeguards for known minor users and tools addressing recommendations, purchases, and time limits, with notice to covered users. Title IV, the SAFE BOTs Act, prohibits false licensed-professional representations by chatbots to known minors, mandates AI and crisis-resource disclosures, and requires policies addressing break prompts after 3 hours and specified harmful content.

Title V mandates FTC, HHS/NIH, and Commerce studies, reports, educational resources, and establishes a Commerce Kids Internet Safety Partnership for 5 years. Section 522 amends subtitle A of the Protecting Children in the 21st Century Act, 15 U.S.C. § 6551 et seq., by replacing §§ 211–214 and 216 with an FTC public-awareness program, 10 years of annual reports, and definitions. Title VI centralizes enforcement, channels constitutional challenges exclusively to the D.C. Circuit with 90- and 60-day limitations periods, preserves COPPA and 47 U.S.C. § 230, protects encryption, bars compelled new age-data collection, includes severability, and sets a default effective date 1 year after enactment.

expert.summary:
### Primary Purpose and Operative Mechanism

H.R. 7757, the "Kids Internet and Digital Safety Act" (or "KIDS Act"), establishes a comprehensive federal regulatory framework to protect minors (defined generally as individuals under age 17) from online harms, obscenity, and exploitative digital features. The bill operates by imposing affirmative compliance obligations, design mandates, and disclosure requirements on operators of commercial websites, online platforms, social media, interactive video games, and artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots. 

---

### Major Provisions by Title

#### Title I: Shielding Minors from Obscenity (SCREEN Act)
*   **Operative Mandate (§ 103):** Effective one year post-enactment, providers of "covered platforms" (publicly accessible platforms where more than one-third of the content is "sexual material harmful to minors" and is knowingly made available) must implement commercially available "technology verification measures" to identify minors and block their access to such material.
*   **Data Minimization and Security (§ 103(b), (d)):** Providers and contracted third parties are prohibited from transferring, disclosing, or retaining verification data beyond what is strictly necessary, and must maintain reasonable administrative, technical, and physical data security practices.
*   **Preemption (§ 106):** Expressly preempts state laws requiring covered platforms to use technology verification measures to prevent minors from accessing harmful sexual material, while preserving state laws governing trespass, contract, tort, product liability, criminal remedies, and general consumer protection.

#### Title II: Addressing Harms to Minors on Online Platforms
*   **Subtitle A (Kids Online Safety Act):** 
    *   *Duty to Address Harms (§ 213):* Mandates that covered platforms establish and enforce policies to address specific harms to minors, including physical violence, sexual exploitation, illicit drug/alcohol/tobacco distribution, and deceptive financial harms. It explicitly disclaims the imposition of a common-law duty of care.
    *   *Safeguards and Default Settings (§ 214):* Requires platforms to provide minors with robust privacy safeguards (e.g., limiting communication, restricting geolocation sharing, and opting out of personalized recommendation systems). Default settings for minors must be set to the most protective level.
    *   *Parental Tools (§ 214(b)):* Mandates parental controls to manage account settings, restrict financial transactions, and monitor screen time. Default settings for children (under age 13) must have parental tools enabled by default.
    *   *Reporting and Audits (§§ 215, 219):* Requires a rapid-response reporting mechanism for online harms (substantive response within 10 days, or faster for imminent threats). Platforms must undergo annual independent third-party audits and submit the results to the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), alongside publishing a redacted public report.
*   **Subtitle B (Safe Messaging for Kids Act):**
    *   *Messaging Prohibitions (§§ 233, 234):* Prohibits platforms from offering ephemeral messaging features to minors, and bans direct messaging features entirely for children under age 13.
    *   *Teen Parental Controls (§ 235):* Mandates parental consent-driven controls for direct messaging used by teens (ages 13–16), including contact-approval notifications and profile-hiding features.
    *   *Effective Date (§ 238):* Subtitle B takes effect 180 days post-enactment, except for the teen parental controls under Section 235 (governed by the general Title VI effective date).
*   **Subtitle C (Stop Profiling Youth and Kids Act):**
    *   *Market Research Ban (§ 243):* Prohibits market or product-focused research on known minors, unless strictly necessary for safety, privacy, or legal compliance. Takes effect 90 days post-enactment (§ 245).

#### Title III: Social Gaming Platforms (Safer GAMING Act)
*   **Communication and Purchase Controls (§ 303):** Requires online video game providers to offer parental controls to restrict verbal, written, or visual communication. These communication safeguards must be enabled and set to the most restrictive settings by default. Providers must also offer tools to restrict in-game purchases and limit gameplay time.

#### Title IV: Artificial Intelligence Chatbots (SAFE BOTs Act)
*   **Prohibitions and Disclosures (§§ 403, 404):** Prohibits chatbot providers from falsely representing that a chatbot is a licensed professional. Mandates clear, age-appropriate disclosures at the first interaction stating that the chatbot is an AI system, and requires suicide prevention hotline resources if a minor prompts the chatbot regarding self-harm.
*   **Usage Policies (§ 405):** Requires policies to prompt minors to take a break after three hours of continuous interaction, and to restrict chatbot promotion of sexual material, gambling, drugs, tobacco, or alcohol.

#### Title V: Research, Education, and Best Practices
*   **Subtitle A (Research):** Directs the FTC, in coordination with the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), to study and report on social media algorithms and minor mental health (§ 512), and minor access to fentanyl via social media (§ 514). Directs the National Institutes of Health (NIH) to conduct a four-year longitudinal study on chatbots and mental health (§ 517).
*   **Subtitle B (Education):** Amends Subtitle A of the Protecting Children in the 21st Century Act (15 U.S.C. 6551 et seq.) by striking sections 211–214 and 216, and inserting new sections 211–213 to mandate a national public awareness campaign and annual reports to Congress (§ 522).
*   **Subtitle C (Partnerships):** Directs the Secretary of Commerce to establish the "Kids Internet Safety Partnership" to identify risks and publish an industry playbook of best practices (§ 526). This partnership sunsets five years post-establishment.

---

### Enforcement, Jurisdiction, and Rules of Construction

*   **FTC Enforcement (§ 601(a)):** Violations are treated as unfair or deceptive acts or practices under Section 18(a)(1)(B) of the FTC Act (15 U.S.C. 57a(a)(1)(B)).
*   **State Attorneys General (§ 601(b)):** Authorizes state attorneys general to bring civil actions *parens patriae* for injunctive relief, compliance, or damages, subject to a prior written notice requirement to the FTC. State actions are barred during the pendency of a parallel federal enforcement action.
*   **Judicial Review (§ 602):** Vests exclusive jurisdiction over constitutional challenges to the Act or actions thereunder in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit. Constitutional challenges to the Act must be filed within 90 days of enactment; challenges to agency actions must be filed within 60 days of the action.
*   **First Amendment and Encryption Protections (§ 603):** Prohibits enforcement based on First Amendment-protected viewpoints. The Act explicitly states it does not require the decryption of communications, the preclusion of end-to-end encryption, or the weakening of any security controls. It further disclaims any requirement for covered platforms to implement age-gating/age-verification functionality (§ 220) or to affirmatively collect age data not kept in the normal course of business (§ 603(11)).
*   **Effective Date (§ 605):** Except as otherwise specified, the Act takes effect one year after the date of enactment.
