This bill is called the Kids Internet and Digital Safety Act, or the KIDS Act. Its main job is to create new rules to protect people under 17 when they are online.

The bill sets up age checks for websites that mostly show sexual material harmful to kids. These sites must use a special tool to figure out if a user is a minor and block them from seeing that content. They cannot keep the personal data used for the age check any longer than necessary. This part starts one year after the bill becomes law.

For social media platforms, the bill requires safety settings. Platforms must offer tools so kids and parents can limit who can message them, stop features that make the app hard to stop using, and control sharing of their location. The default setting must be the most private and safe choice. Platforms must also give parents a way to see and change their child's privacy settings and screen time. Platforms have to hire an outside auditor every year to check how they are doing and make a public report within 45 days of finishing.

The bill bans disappearing messages for all minors. It bans direct messaging for kids under 13. For teens 13 and older, platforms must give parents controls to approve contacts and manage who can message them. It stops platforms from studying minors like test subjects for market research, unless it is to make the platform safer. These changes take effect between 90 and 180 days after the bill becomes law.

For online video games that connect to the internet, the bill says the game provider must give parents tools to limit who their child talks to, restrict purchases, and set time limits. These safety controls must be turned on and set to the most protective level by default.

The bill also makes rules for AI chatbots. A chatbot must tell a minor that it is not a real person and suggest a break if a chat has lasted for three hours. It must also provide a suicide prevention hotline number if asked about suicide. A chatbot cannot lie and say it is a doctor or other licensed professional.

The law asks for several government studies. These include a study on how social media affects kids' mental health, a report on whether minors can buy dangerous drugs like fentanyl through social media, and a four-year study on how chatbots affect kids' loneliness and anxiety. It also creates a public education campaign to teach online safety and a special partnership to share best practices.

The general rules of the bill start one year after it is passed. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general can enforce the law.

crs_reference.summary:
Kids Internet and Digital Safety Act or the KIDS Act
This bill requires specified online platforms to establish safeguards for minors. The safeguards include (1) limiting access to specified sexual material, (2) providing parental controls on social media and online video game platforms, and (3) requiring artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots to disclose certain information to users who are minors.
First, publicly available online platforms on which more than one-third of the content is considered sexual material harmful to minors under the bill must adopt technology to identify minors and prevent them from accessing such material.
Next, social media platforms must (1) implement default settings for minors that limit compulsive usage features and the ability of other users to communicate with minors, and (2) provide tools for parents to manage the privacy and account settings of a minor. Social media platforms may not allow ephemeral messaging features for minors.
The bill also requires online video game platforms to provide tools that allow parents to (1) limit communication between a minor and other users of the platform, and (2) restrict purchases by a minor on the platform. 
Further, providers of AI chatbots must disclose to users who are minors (1) that the chatbot is an AI system and not a human, and (2) suicide and crisis intervention hotline information.
Finally, the bill requires specified studies and reports about the effects of social media platforms on minors and provides for enforcement of the bill's requirements by the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general.

anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.summary:
The "Removing Barriers to Work for Disabled Americans Act" (H.R. 8884) amends Title II of the Social Security Act to reauthorize the Social Security Administration's authority to conduct experiments and demonstration projects related to the disability insurance program. This demonstration authority had previously lapsed (set to expire in 2021–2022 under prior law).

The bill makes several specific changes:

- **Reauthorization timeline:** It extends the authority to initiate demonstration projects through December 31, 2030, and sets the authority to carry out such projects to terminate on December 31, 2031.

- **Waiver authority:** It extends through December 31, 2030, the Commissioner's authority to waive compliance with certain benefit requirements when conducting projects. It also lengthens the advance notice period to Congress from 90 days to 120 days, and requires that the report describing a project include the evaluation metrics to be used.

- **Funding source:** It revises how costs are paid. Administrative expenditures for these projects are to come from funds available for administering Title II. Benefits payable to individuals participating in the projects are to be paid from either the Federal Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund or the Federal Disability Insurance Trust Fund, as the Commissioner determines appropriate.

- **Participant protection:** It adds a new requirement that any project must ensure that a participant's total income will not be reduced because of their participation.

- **Technical amendments:** It corrects a reference in the statute and strikes subsection (f) of Section 234.

The amendments made by the bill take effect on January 1, 2027.

The bill was introduced May 19, 2026, by Mr. Austin Scott of Georgia, referred to the Committee on Ways and Means, and reported with an amendment on June 25, 2026.

The government sometimes runs test programs, called "demonstration projects." These are like experiments to try new ideas and see if they work better. The rules that let the government run these tests had already ended years ago.

The text summarized is the version reported with an amendment (which struck all after the enacting clause and substituted new text) and referred to the Committee of the Whole.

Section 2(a) amends section 234(d)(2) to extend the authority to initiate demonstration projects from the expired December 31, 2021 date to December 31, 2030, and to extend the termination date for carrying out such projects from December 31, 2022 to December 31, 2031.

Section 2(b) amends section 234(c) (the authority to waive compliance with benefits requirements) by conforming the operative date to December 31, 2030; by extending the advance-notice period to Congress from 90 days to 120 days; and by adding a requirement that the report to Congress include the "evaluation metrics to be used" with respect to the experiment or demonstration project.

Section 2(c) revises section 201(k) (42 U.S.C. 401(k)) in its entirety, providing that administrative expenditures for section 234 experiments and demonstration projects be paid from funds made available for administration of title II, and that benefits payable by reason of participation be paid from either the Federal Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund or the Federal Disability Insurance Trust Fund, as the Commissioner determines appropriate.

Section 2(d) amends section 234(e) to add a new paragraph (4), imposing a limitation that a participating individual's total income will not be reduced due to participation in an experiment or demonstration project, with conforming punctuation changes to paragraphs (2) and (3).

Section 2(e) makes technical amendments: in subsection (d)(1), substituting "section" for "subsection," and striking subsection (f) in its entirety.

Section 2(f) provides that the amendments made by section 2 take effect on January 1, 2027.

The bill operates as a reauthorization and amendment of existing demonstration authority rather than a new appropriation; funding is drawn from existing administrative appropriations and the specified trust funds. The extension effectively revives lapsed authority (which expired in 2021–2022) prospectively.

Removing Barriers to Work for Disabled Americans Act
This bill reauthorizes through 2031 the Social Security Administration’s (SSA’s) authority to carry out demonstration projects within the Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) program. The bill also imposes requirements related to beneficiary income, project funding, and SSA reporting.
SSDI demonstration projects must be designed to promote attachment to the workforce and generally involve temporary changes to SSDI policies tested on a subset of beneficiaries. Participation in a demonstration project must be voluntary. SSA’s authority to carry out these projects expired on December 31, 2022.
Under the bill, SSA must ensure that an individual’s participation in a demonstration project does not reduce their total income. Further, the bill specifies that administrative expenses related to demonstration projects must be paid from funds appropriated for administration.
Finally, the bill requires SSA to report to Congress 120 days before initiating a demonstration project. This is an increase from 90 days under current law. This advance notification must include evaluation metrics for the relevant project.

anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.summary:
The Florida Freeze Disaster Assistance Act of 2026 (H.R. 9094) appropriates funds for the Secretary of Agriculture to provide disaster relief to states for agricultural losses caused by freezes or cold weather.

The bill appropriates $3.5 billion from the U.S. Treasury for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2027, as an additional amount for the "Office of the Secretary" of the U.S. Department of Agriculture. These funds would remain available until expended.

The money is to be distributed as block grants to states to compensate for losses of revenue, quality, or production of crops (including crops prevented from being planted), as well as trees, bushes, and vines, when those losses result from a freeze or cold weather condition. The assistance must include compensation to producers for losses of multi-year crops.

Eligibility for the funds is limited in two key ways. First, the funds may be used exclusively for losses occurring in counties that received a disaster designation for freeze and related cold weather conditions issued by the Secretary on March 4, 2026. Second, the funds are made available only upon the request of a state department of agriculture or another appropriate state agency as determined by the Secretary.

The bill requires the Secretary to submit a report to the Committees on Appropriations of the House and Senate describing how the assistance is being implemented. The first report is due no later than 120 days after the bill's enactment, with additional reports each fiscal quarter thereafter until the appropriated funds are expended.

The appropriated amount is designated by Congress as an emergency requirement under section 251(b)(2)(A)(i) of the Balanced Budget and Emergency Deficit Control Act of 1985.

The bill was introduced in the House on June 2, 2026, and referred to the Committee on Appropriations and the Committee on the Budget.

expert.summary:
The Florida Freeze Disaster Assistance Act of 2026 (H.R. 9094) is a single-purpose appropriations measure directing federal disaster assistance for agricultural losses attributable to freeze or cold weather conditions.

Section 1 provides the short title. Section 2 appropriates $3,500,000,000 out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2027, as an additional amount for the "Office of the Secretary" account of the U.S. Department of Agriculture. The funds are made available until expended (no-year availability). This is a direct appropriation, not merely an authorization.

The operative mechanism directs the Secretary of Agriculture to provide the assistance in the form of block grants to States. Eligible losses encompass revenue, quality, or production of crops (including crops prevented from planting), trees, bushes, and vines resulting from a freeze or cold weather condition. A proviso mandates that the assistance include compensation to producers for losses of multi-year crops.

The appropriation is subject to several conditions established through provisos:

- Geographic/eligibility limitation: Funds are made available exclusively for losses occurring in counties that received a disaster designation for freeze and related cold weather conditions issued by the Secretary on March 4, 2026. This ties eligibility to a specific, already-issued designation rather than a prospective or general standard.

- Disbursement condition precedent: Funds are made available only upon the request of a State department of agriculture, or other appropriate State agency as determined by the Secretary.

- Reporting requirement: Not later than 120 days after the date of enactment, and for each fiscal quarter thereafter until the appropriated amounts are expended, the Secretary must submit a report to the House and Senate Committees on Appropriations describing implementation of the assistance.

- Budget-enforcement designation: The amount is designated by Congress as an emergency requirement pursuant to section 251(b)(2)(A)(i) of the Balanced Budget and Emergency Deficit Control Act of 1985, which exempts the spending from applicable discretionary spending limits/adjusts caps accordingly.

The bill does not amend any existing provision of the U.S. Code or any named authorizing statute, does not prescribe formulas or per-State allocation criteria, and does not establish sunset provisions beyond the fiscal-year designation and the until-expended availability. It contains no effective-date provision, taking effect upon enactment. The bill was referred to the Committee on Appropriations and additionally to the Committee on the Budget for provisions within their respective jurisdictions.

anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.summary:
The Secure America Act (Public Law 119-98), enacted June 10, 2026, is a budget reconciliation measure that provides supplemental appropriations for fiscal year 2026 to fund border security, immigration enforcement, and related Department of Homeland Security operations. All funds appropriated remain available until September 30, 2029.

The Act is divided into two titles. Title I, under the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, appropriates funds for functions other than immigration and customs enforcement:
- $9.55 billion to U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to hire, pay, train, and equip Border Patrol agents and support personnel. None of these funds may be used to recruit, hire, or train "processing coordinators" after October 31, 2028.
- $7.45 billion to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) for Homeland Security Investigations personnel and operations, of which $108.5 million is designated for additional child exploitation investigators and forensic analysts to support identifying and rescuing victims of child sexual exploitation.
- $3.45 billion to CBP for inspection equipment, air and marine platforms, border surveillance technology, the biometric entry-and-exit system, and combating drug trafficking. Funds may not be used for surveillance towers that have not been tested and accepted as delivering "autonomous" capabilities (defined as systems using AI or similar algorithms to detect and track items without continuous human control).
- $2.5 billion to the Secretary of Homeland Security for the title's purposes.

Title II, under the Committee on the Judiciary, funds immigration enforcement:
- $13.02 billion to CBP for hiring, equipping, and supporting agents to carry out immigration enforcement.
- $31.075 billion to ICE for personnel, transportation, removal operations, information technology, facilities, fleet, 287(g) agreements with state and local authorities, and legal staff. At least $350 million is designated for detainer management and arrests of "covered unlawful aliens" (defined to include certain inadmissible, deportable, or criminally charged aliens) in jurisdictions that are not "qualified cooperating jurisdictions"; Indian tribal governments are excluded from that category. These funds generally may not be used to release such aliens except as required by existing law.
- $2.5 billion to the Secretary of Homeland Security for the title's purposes.

This law is called the "Secure America Act." It gives money to the government to work on America's borders. The money comes from the U.S. Treasury, which is where the country keeps its money.

Here are the big amounts of money the law gives out. All of it can be used until September 30, 2029.

- $9.55 billion to hire, pay, train, and equip Border Patrol agents and helpers.
- $7.45 billion for Homeland Security Investigations agents. Part of this ($108.5 million) is to help find and rescue children who are hurt or abused.
- $3.45 billion for new tools and technology. This includes machines that scan for illegal drugs like fentanyl, better planes and boats, and cameras to watch the borders.
- $13.02 billion to hire and train border officers to do immigration work. Immigration means the rules about who can come into the country.
- $31.075 billion for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (called ICE). This pays for workers, moving people out of the country, computers, buildings, and cars.

Part of the ICE money (at least $350 million) is for arresting certain people who broke the law and are living here without permission.

The law also sets some rules. For example, money can't be used for camera towers that were not tested and accepted.

The President approved this law on June 10, 2026.

expert.summary:
The Secure America Act (Pub. L. 119-98, S. 2, enacted June 10, 2026) is a budget reconciliation measure enacted pursuant to title II of S. Con. Res. 33. Its operative mechanism is the direct appropriation of supplemental funds—each drawn "out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated," in addition to amounts otherwise available—for fiscal year 2026 to Department of Homeland Security components, all remaining available until September 30, 2029. The Act contains no substantive amendments to the U.S. Code; it operates entirely through appropriations, referencing existing statutory provisions only to define or condition fund use.

Title I (Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee) appropriates: (1) under section 101, $9,550,000,000 to the CBP Commissioner to hire, pay, train, and equip Border Patrol agents and support personnel for functions "other than immigration enforcement and customs functions," with a restriction (§101(b)) barring use of such funds to recruit, hire, or train processing coordinators after October 31, 2028; (2) under section 102, $7,450,000,000 to the ICE Director for Homeland Security Investigations personnel and operations, of which $108,500,000 is earmarked for child exploitation investigators and forensics analysts, again limited to functions other than immigration/customs enforcement; (3) under section 103, $3,450,000,000 to CBP for nonintrusive inspection equipment, Air and Marine platforms, border surveillance technology, the biometric entry-exit system under section 7208 of the Intelligence Reform and Terrorism Prevention Act of 2004 (8 U.S.C. 1365b), and drug-interdiction, with a restriction (§103(b)) barring procurement or deployment of surveillance towers not tested and accepted to deliver "autonomous" capabilities (defined in §103(c)); and (4) under section 104, $2,500,000,000 to the DHS Secretary for title I purposes.

Title II (Judiciary Committee) appropriates: (1) under section 201, $13,020,000,000 to CBP for personnel and support to carry out immigration enforcement activities; (2) under section 202, $31,075,000,000 to ICE for nine enumerated purposes, including personnel, removal transportation, information technology, facility and fleet maintenance, expansion of 287(g) agreements under section 287(g) INA (8 U.S.C. 1357(g)), and the Office of the Principal Legal Advisor. Section 202(9) directs not less than $350,000,000 for arrest and detainer operations targeting "covered unlawful aliens" (defined in §202(9)(D) by reference to INA §§ 236(c)(1), 212(a)(2), 237(a)(2), 236/241(a)/287, and 275/276) encountered in jurisdictions that are not "qualified cooperating jurisdictions" (defined via 287(g) agreements or certified compliance with 8 U.S.C. 1373 and 1644), with Indian tribal governments excluded, and a limitation (§202(9)(C)) barring use of such funds to facilitate release except as required by existing law. Section 203 appropriates $2,500,000,000 to the DHS Secretary for title II purposes or paragraphs (3) or (7) of section 100051 of Public Law 119-21.

The Secure America Act provides additional fiscal year 2026 appropriations to the Department of Homeland Security, primarily for U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), with most funds available through September 30, 2029.

The Act appropriates $9.55 billion to CBP to hire, pay, train, and equip Border Patrol agents and support personnel for functions other than immigration enforcement and customs functions. These funds may not be used after October 31, 2028, to recruit, hire, or train personnel for processing coordinator duties. It also appropriates $3.45 billion to CBP for border security technology and screening, including nonintrusive inspection equipment, artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies, air and marine response platforms, border surveillance technology, biometric entry and exit system expenses, drug trafficking interdiction, and mission support not related to immigration or customs enforcement. Funds may not be used for surveillance towers along the southwest or northern borders unless CBP has tested and accepted them to deliver autonomous capabilities, as defined in the Act.

The Act appropriates $7.45 billion to ICE for Homeland Security Investigations personnel and mission support for functions other than immigration or customs enforcement. Of that amount, $108.5 million is designated for child exploitation investigators, forensic analysts, victim identification, rescue support, and related training.

For immigration enforcement, the Act appropriates $13.02 billion to CBP and $31.075 billion to ICE for personnel, transportation for removals, information technology, facilities, fleet needs, 287(g) agreements with state and local authorities, legal staff, and other enforcement operations. At least $350 million of ICE’s funding must support operations involving specified “covered unlawful aliens” in jurisdictions that are not “qualified cooperating jurisdictions,” with Indian tribal governments excluded from that category. The Act also provides two separate $2.5 billion appropriations to the Secretary of Homeland Security for purposes specified in the Act.

expert.summary:
### Legislative Summary: Secure America Act (P.L. 119-98)

#### Primary Purpose and Operative Mechanism
The Secure America Act (S. 2) is a budget reconciliation act enacted pursuant to S. Con. Res. 33 (119th Congress). Its primary purpose is to provide supplemental fiscal year (FY) 2026 appropriations to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) for border security, technology procurement, non-immigration law enforcement, and immigration enforcement operations. The operative mechanism of the Act is the direct appropriation of mandatory funds out of the Treasury, totaling $69.495 billion, made available through September 30, 2029, subject to specific statutory restrictions, exclusions, and conditions precedent.

---

#### Title I: Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs
Title I appropriates $22.95 billion for non-immigration enforcement and non-customs functions, border technology, and general departmental support.

*   **Section 101 (U.S. Customs and Border Protection Personnel):** Appropriates $9.55 billion to the Commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to hire, pay, train, and equip Border Patrol agents and support personnel. 
    *   *Statutory Restriction:* Funds are restricted to personnel conducting functions other than immigration enforcement and customs functions.
    *   *Sunset Provision:* None of the funds may be used to recruit, hire, or train personnel for processing coordinator duties after October 31, 2028.
*   **Section 102 (U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement):** Appropriates $7.45 billion to the Director of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) for Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) personnel, mission support, and operations.
    *   *Earmark:* Allocates $108.5 million specifically for child exploitation investigators and forensics analysts at the HSI Child Exploitation Investigations Unit's Victim Identification Laboratory and offices of the Special Agent in Charge, and for training state and local law enforcement at the HSI Cyber Crimes Center.
    *   *Statutory Restriction:* Excludes the use of these funds for HSI's immigration enforcement and customs enforcement missions.
*   **Section 103 (Border Security, Technology, and Screening):** Appropriates $3.45 billion to the CBP Commissioner for technology procurement, upgrades, and operations. Eligible activities include:
    1.  Nonintrusive inspection equipment and civil works (including artificial intelligence [AI] and machine learning [ML]) to combat illicit narcotics at ports of entry and borders.
    2.  Air and Marine Operations platform upgrades.
    3.  Border surveillance technology upgrades.
    4.  Biometric entry and exit system expenses under section 7208 of the Intelligence Reform and Terrorism Prevention Act of 2004 (8 U.S.C. § 1365b).
    5.  Counter-drug trafficking operations (specifically targeting fentanyl and precursors).
    6.  CBP mission support and operations for non-immigration and non-customs functions.
    *   *Condition Precedent:* Prohibits procurement or deployment of surveillance towers along the southwest and northern borders unless CBP has tested and accepted them to deliver "autonomous" capabilities (defined as systems applying AI, ML, computer vision, or other algorithms to detect, identify, classify, and track items in real time without active human command or control).
*   **Section 104 (Additional DHS Appropriations):** Appropriates $2.5 billion to the Secretary of Homeland Security for the purposes authorized under Title I.

---

#### Title II: Committee on the Judiciary
Title II appropriates $46.595 billion specifically dedicated to immigration enforcement, detention, and removal operations.

*   **Section 201 (U.S. Customs and Border Protection):** Appropriates $13.02 billion to the CBP Commissioner to hire, pay, train, and equip CBP agents and support staff, and for mission support and operations, specifically to carry out immigration enforcement activities.
*   **Section 202 (U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement):** Appropriates $31.075 billion to the ICE Director for immigration enforcement and removal operations, categorized into nine authorized purposes:
    1.  Hiring, paying, training, and equipping ICE personnel across all directorates.
    2.  Transportation and related costs for alien departure and removal operations.
    3.  Information technology maintenance, including body-worn cameras and fee collections.
    4.  Facility maintenance and sustainment.
    5.  Fleet maintenance and sustainment.
    6.  Expansion and implementation of joint state/local enforcement agreements under section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) (8 U.S.C. § 1357(g)).
    7.  Hiring and paying attorneys and support staff within the Office of the Principal Legal Advisor (OPLA) for representation in enforcement and removal proceedings.
    8.  General ICE mission support, awards, and operations.
    9.  *Arrests of Released Covered Unlawful Aliens:* Allocates a minimum of $350 million for detainer management, detainer issuance, custodial transfer, release monitoring, transportation, and arrests of "covered unlawful aliens" encountered in jurisdictions that are not "qualified cooperating jurisdictions."
        *   *Exception:* Indian tribal governments are exempt from being classified as non-cooperating jurisdictions.
        *   *Statutory Definitions:* 
            *   "Qualified cooperating jurisdiction" is defined as a State or political subdivision that, as of the enactment date, has an active INA § 287(g) agreement, or has filed a certification of compliance with section 642 of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 (8 U.S.C. § 1373) and section 434 of the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996 (8 U.S.C. § 1644).
            *   "Covered unlawful alien" is defined as an adult alien who is subject to mandatory detention under INA § 236(c)(1) (8 U.S.C. § 1226(c)(1)); inadmissible under INA § 212(a)(2) (8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(2)); deportable under INA § 237(a)(2) (8 U.S.C. § 1227(a)(2)); the subject of an immigration detainer or custody request under INA §§ 236, 241(a), or 287 following an arrest or conviction for a non-minor criminal offense; or charged with/convicted of illegal entry or reentry under INA §§ 275 or 276 (8 U.S.C. §§ 1325, 1326).
        *   *Funding Limitation:* Except as required by existing law, no funds appropriated under this paragraph may be used to release, parole, place on alternatives to detention, or facilitate the release of any encountered covered unlawful alien.
*   **Section 203 (Additional DHS Appropriations):** Appropriates $2.5 billion to the Secretary of Homeland Security, available for Title II purposes or for purposes specified in paragraphs (3) or (7) of section 100051 of Public Law 119-21.

eli5.summary:
This bill, called the Secure America Act, gives a lot of money to parts of the government that work on border security and immigration. It provides funds for the 2026 budget year, and the money can be spent until September 30, 2029.

The bill gives money to two main agencies. U.S. Customs and Border Protection gets funds to hire, train, and equip Border Patrol agents and to buy new technology. This includes money for inspection machines, surveillance tools, and systems to check fingerprints or faces at borders. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement gets money to hire more agents, investigators, and lawyers. It also pays for things like transporting people, maintaining buildings and vehicles, and upgrading computers.

A large part of the money for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is set aside for arresting and managing certain adults who are in the country without legal permission and have been charged with or convicted of crimes. At least $350 million is specifically for operations in places that do not have a formal cooperation agreement with immigration authorities. The bill says this money generally cannot be used to release these individuals into the community. It also sets aside over $108 million to hire special investigators focused on rescuing children from exploitation and abuse.

expert.summary:
The Secure America Act provides for direct appropriations to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) for fiscal year 2026, enacted as reconciliation legislation pursuant to S. Con. Res. 33. The Act’s operative mechanism is supplemental, multi-year appropriations—available until September 30, 2029—drawn from the general fund, with purpose-specific use restrictions.

Title I (Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs):
Section 101 appropriates $9,550,000,000 to the Commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to hire, pay, train, and equip Border Patrol agents and support personnel for functions other than immigration enforcement and customs functions, with a restriction that after October 31, 2028, none of the funds may be used to recruit, hire, or train processing coordinators.
Section 102 appropriates $7,450,000,000 to the Director of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) for Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents, support personnel, and necessary expenses for HSI mission support and operations and maintenance, explicitly excluding immigration and customs enforcement missions. Of this amount, $108,500,000 is directed to hiring and equipping additional child exploitation investigators and forensics analysts at specified HSI units and for related training, including for state and local law enforcement.
Section 103 appropriates $3,450,000,000 to the CBP Commissioner for enumerated purposes: procurement and integration of nonintrusive inspection equipment with AI and machine learning; upgrading air and marine platforms; border surveillance technology procurement; expenses for the biometric entry-exit system under 8 U.S.C. 1365b; combating drug trafficking, including fentanyl and precursors; and mission support and operations and maintenance for non-immigration and non-customs functions. It restricts procurement or deployment of autonomous surveillance towers not meeting CBP testing and acceptance standards and defines “autonomous” as a system applying specified algorithms that can make operational adjustments without active personnel engagement or continuous human control.
Section 104 appropriates $2,500,000,000 to the Secretary of Homeland Security for the purposes of Title I.

Title II (Committee on the Judiciary):
Section 201 appropriates $13,020,000,000 to the CBP Commissioner for hiring, paying, training, and equipping CBP agents and support staff and for mission support and operations and maintenance to carry out immigration enforcement activities.
Section 202 appropriates $31,075,000,000 to the ICE Director for nine specified immigration enforcement purposes: personnel hiring and equipping across all directorates; transportation for removals; information technology; facility and fleet maintenance; expanding section 287(g) agreements (8 U.S.C. 1357(g)); hiring attorneys for the Office of the Principal Legal Advisor; mission support and operations and maintenance; and, within this amount, not less than $350,000,000 for operations to arrest covered unlawful aliens encountered in jurisdictions that are not qualified cooperating jurisdictions, subject to a limitation prohibiting the use of such funds to release or facilitate release of any covered unlawful alien. The term “qualified cooperating jurisdiction” is defined as a State or political subdivision that either has an active 287(g) agreement or has certified compliance with 8 U.S.C. 1373 and 8 U.S.C. 1644; Indian tribal governments are excluded from treatment as non-qualified. “Covered unlawful alien” is defined by cross-reference to criminal and security-related inadmissibility and deportability grounds, certain immigration detainers following criminal arrests, and aliens charged with or convicted of offenses under 8 U.S.C. 1325 or 1326.
Section 203 appropriates $2,500,000,000 to the Secretary of Homeland Security for the purposes of Title II or specific paragraphs in Public Law 119-21.

The Aerial Firefighting Enhancement Act of 2025 (Public Law 119-18) amends the Wildfire Suppression Aircraft Transfer Act of 1996 to reauthorize and modify the Department of Defense's authority to sell aircraft and related parts for wildfire suppression purposes.

The bill makes several changes to existing law. First, it expands the permitted use of the aircraft by adding references to "water" alongside the existing references to "fire retardant," so that aircraft sold under this authority may be used to deliver water in addition to fire retardant. Second, it revises the restriction on how sold aircraft may be used, providing that such aircraft "may be used only for the provision of aircraft services for wildfire suppression purposes."

The bill also makes a technical cross-reference correction within the law and replaces the provision governing the time period during which the sale authority may be exercised. Under the new language, the authority begins on the date the Aerial Firefighting Enhancement Act of 2025 is enacted (June 12, 2025) and ends on October 1, 2035.

The Act was passed by the Senate on April 8, 2025, passed by the House on June 3, 2025, and approved on June 12, 2025.

The old law let the Department of Defense (the part of the government in charge of the military) sell airplanes and airplane parts. These planes and parts are used to help put out wildfires.

Second, the old law talked about airplanes that drop "fire retardant." Fire retardant is a special material that helps stop fires from spreading. The new law adds the word "water" too. So now the planes can also be used to drop water on fires.

expert.summary:
This enacted measure (Pub. L. 119-18, S. 160), the "Aerial Firefighting Enhancement Act of 2025," amends the Wildfire Suppression Aircraft Transfer Act of 1996 (Pub. L. 104-307; codified as a note to 10 U.S.C. 2576) to reauthorize and modify the Department of Defense's authority to sell aircraft and parts for wildfire suppression purposes. The operative mechanism is a series of amendments to Section 2 of the 1996 Act.

Section 1 provides the short title (10 U.S.C. 101 note).

Section 2 makes five amendments:

(1) In subsection (a)(1), a conforming change strikes "a period" and inserts "the period," and expands the authorized delivery mechanism by inserting "or water" after "fire retardant," thereby extending the covered use to aircraft equipped for water delivery in addition to fire retardant.

(2) Subsection (b) is rewritten so that aircraft and parts sold under subsection (a) "may be used only for the provision of aircraft services for wildfire suppression purposes," replacing the prior use-restriction language.

(3) Subsection (c) is likewise amended to insert "or water" after "fire retardant."

(4) In the second sentence of subsection (d)(1), the cross-reference to "subsection (a)(1)" is replaced with "subsection (g)," conforming the internal reference to the relocated authority period.

(5) Subsection (g) is struck and replaced with a new "Period for Exercise of Authority" provision establishing that the authority runs from the date of enactment of the Aerial Firefighting Enhancement Act of 2025 through October 1, 2035—effectively a reauthorization with a fixed sunset date of October 1, 2035.

The Act contains no appropriations and provides no separate authorization of appropriations; it operates solely as a reauthorization and modification of existing DoD sale authority. No separate effective date is specified beyond the date of enactment, which governs the commencement of the authority period under new subsection (g).

The bill was approved June 12, 2025. Legislative history: S. 160 was considered and passed by the Senate on April 8, 2025, and considered and passed by the House on June 3, 2025 (Cong. Rec. Vol. 171 (2025)).

anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.label: anthropic/claude-opus-4.8
anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.summary:
The ACES Act of 2025 (Public Law 119-32) directs a study on the rates of cancer occurrence and death among former military aircrew members. Its primary purpose is to have the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine examine whether individuals who served as active duty aircrew in the Armed Forces experience elevated cancer prevalence and mortality.

The Act requires the Secretary of Veterans Affairs, within 30 days of enactment, to seek an agreement with the National Academies to conduct the study. The Secretary must finalize that agreement within 60 days of beginning negotiations. If the Secretary fails to meet this deadline, the Secretary must report to the Senate and House Committees on Veterans' Affairs explaining the failure and estimating a finalization date, and must provide progress briefings to those committees at least every 60 days thereafter.

The study must: (1) identify exposures associated with the military occupations of covered individuals, including chemicals, compounds, agents, and other phenomena; (2) review existing literature to determine associations between those exposures and overall cancer morbidity and mortality, as well as specific cancers—brain, colon and rectal, kidney, lung, melanoma skin cancer, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, pancreatic, prostate, testicular, thyroid, urinary bladder, and other cancers the Secretary deems appropriate in consultation with the National Academies; and (3) determine, where possible, the prevalence of and mortality from those cancers among covered individuals using available data sources. Such sources may include administrative and health care databases of the Departments of Veterans Affairs and Defense and the individual Services, the National Death Index maintained by the CDC's National Center for Health Statistics, and a prior study conducted under the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021.

Upon completion, the National Academies must submit a report of the results to the Secretary and the two Veterans' Affairs committees.

A "covered individual" is defined as someone who served on active duty in the Army, Navy, Air Force, or Marine Corps as an aircrew member of a fixed-wing aircraft, including pilots, navigators, weapons systems operators, aircraft system operators, or any other crew member who regularly flew in a fixed-wing aircraft.

The ACES Act of 2025 (Pub. L. 119-32, S. 201, enacted August 14, 2025) directs the commissioning of an independent epidemiological study on cancer prevalence and mortality among former active duty fixed-wing aircrew. The Act is freestanding legislation; it does not amend title 38 or other existing U.S. Code provisions.

Section 1 provides the short title. Section 2 constitutes the operative provision.

Section 2(a) directs the Secretary of Veterans Affairs, not later than 30 days after enactment, to "seek to enter into" an agreement with the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine to conduct the study. This is a duty to seek an agreement rather than an unqualified mandate to execute one. Under subsection (a)(2)(A), the Secretary must finalize the agreement within 60 days after entering negotiations. Subsection (a)(2)(B) establishes a fallback reporting mechanism triggered by failure to meet the 60-day deadline: the Secretary must submit to the Senate and House Committees on Veterans' Affairs a report explaining the failure and estimating a finalization date, and must provide progress briefings to those committees not less frequently than every 60 days thereafter.

Section 2(b) prescribes the study's scope. The National Academies shall (1) identify exposures associated with covered individuals' military occupations, including chemicals, compounds, agents, and other phenomena; (2) conduct a literature review of associations between such exposures and overall cancer morbidity and mortality and the incidence/prevalence of twelve enumerated cancers (brain, colon and rectal, kidney, lung, melanoma skin, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, pancreatic, prostate, testicular, thyroid, urinary bladder), plus other cancers the Secretary designates in consultation with the National Academies; and (3) determine, to the extent possible, prevalence and mortality among covered individuals using available data sources, which may include VA, DoD, and Service administrative and health databases, the National Death Index maintained by the CDC's National Center for Health Statistics, and the study conducted under section 750 of the William M. (Mac) Thornberry National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021 (Pub. L. 116-283, 134 Stat. 3716).

Section 2(c) requires the National Academies, at the study's conclusion, to submit a report of results to the Secretary and the two Veterans' Affairs Committees. No deadline is fixed for study completion or the final report.

Section 2(d) defines "covered individual" as a person who served on active duty in the Army, Navy, Air Force, or Marine Corps as a fixed-wing aircrew member—including pilot, navigator, weapons systems operator, aircraft system operator, or any other crew member who regularly flew in a fixed-wing aircraft.

The Act contains no authorization of appropriations or appropriation of funds.

anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.label: anthropic/claude-opus-4.8
anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.summary:
The "Ending Improper Payments to Deceased People Act" (Public Law 119-77) amends Section 205(r) of the Social Security Act to improve coordination between the Social Security Administration, federal and state agencies, and the federal "Do Not Pay" working system, with the goal of reducing improper payments to deceased individuals.

The bill directs the Commissioner of Social Security to provide death information (collected under paragraph (1) of the same section) to the agency operating the Do Not Pay working system, "to the extent feasible." This data sharing is intended to help prevent improper payments and support the recovery of payments that were improperly made. The sharing must occur through a cooperative arrangement that meets existing statutory requirements (subparagraphs (A) and (B) of paragraph (3)). While data is being provided, the Commissioner and the Do Not Pay agency must enter into an agreement, based on an agreed-upon methodology, covering the proportional share of state death data costs; this agreement may be periodically reviewed.

The bill adds a new provision (paragraph (12)) barring the Commissioner from recording a death on a shareable record for any individual unless the Commissioner finds "clear and convincing evidence" supporting that the individual should be presumed deceased.

To address individuals who are incorrectly identified as deceased, the bill amends paragraph (7) to require the Commissioner, upon learning of such an error, to notify any agency that has a cooperative arrangement under paragraph (3) or (11) of the error.

These amendments take effect on December 27, 2026. The Act itself was approved on February 10, 2026.

This law is called the "Ending Improper Payments to Deceased People Act." It tries to stop the government from sending money to people who have died.

Here is how it works. The government keeps a list of people who have passed away. This list is kept by the Social Security office. Social Security helps people, like older people, by giving them money.

There is also a special computer system called "Do Not Pay." Its job is to help stop payments that should not be made, and to get back money that was paid by mistake.

The new law says the head of Social Security should share death information with the Do Not Pay system when they can. This helps stop the wrong payments. The two groups must make a deal about how to share the cost of getting death records from states.

The law also says something important. Social Security cannot mark someone as dead unless there is very strong proof that the person really died. This helps stop mistakes.

Sometimes a living person gets marked as dead by accident. If that happens, the law says Social Security must tell the other groups it works with about the mistake. That way the error can be fixed.

This law was approved on February 10, 2026. The changes will start on December 27, 2026.

expert.summary:
**Summary of Public Law 119-77 ("Ending Improper Payments to Deceased People Act")**

This enacted bill (S. 269, signed February 10, 2026) amends section 205(r) of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. 405(r)) to improve coordination between the Social Security Administration (SSA) and the Do Not Pay working system described in 31 U.S.C. 3354(c) with respect to death data, for the purpose of preventing and recovering improper payments.

**Section 2(a)** strikes existing paragraph (11) of section 205(r)—as previously amended by section 801(a)(7) of title VIII of division FF of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021 (Pub. L. 116-260)—and substitutes two new paragraphs:

- *New paragraph (11)* directs the Commissioner of Social Security, "to the extent feasible," to provide death information furnished under paragraph (1) to the agency operating the Do Not Pay working system for that system's authorized uses, through a cooperative arrangement, conditioned on satisfaction of the requirements of subparagraphs (A) and (B) of paragraph (3). It further mandates that, while data is being provided, the Commissioner and the operating agency enter into an agreement based on an agreed-upon methodology covering the proportional share of State death data costs, subject to periodic review.

- *New paragraph (12)* prohibits the Commissioner from recording a death to a providable record for any individual absent "clear and convincing evidence" supporting a presumption that the individual is deceased.

**Section 2(b)** amends section 205(r)(7) (added by section 801(a)(4) of the same 2021 Act) by adding a new subparagraph (C) requiring the Commissioner, upon identifying an individual incorrectly identified as deceased, to notify any agency holding a cooperative arrangement with the Commissioner under paragraph (3) or (11) of the error. This supplements existing subparagraphs (A) and (B) (conforming "and"/punctuation amendments effected).

**Effective date (Section 2(c)):** The amendments made by section 2 take effect December 27, 2026—a date later than the Act's February 10, 2026 approval date, establishing a delayed effective date.

The bill contains no appropriations; it establishes operative directives and a cost-sharing agreement requirement but does not authorize or appropriate funds. It includes no sunset provision. Notable conditions precedent include the feasibility qualifier on data-sharing, the paragraph (3)(A)–(B) prerequisites for the cooperative arrangement, and the clear-and-convincing-evidence evidentiary standard governing recordation of deaths.

Ending Improper Payments to Deceased People Act
This act permanently allows the Department of the Treasury to access certain death records maintained by the Social Security Administration (SSA) to help prevent and recover improper payments (e.g., payments to deceased individuals). The act also establishes evidentiary requirements the SSA must meet before identifying an individual as deceased.
Current law requires the SSA to share its Death Master File with the Do Not Pay system maintained by Treasury for three years. The act makes this requirement permanent. Treasury must enter into an agreement with the SSA related to Treasury's share of the cost of state death data.
The act also prohibits the SSA from recording a death in the master file unless the SSA has clear and convincing evidence that the individual should be presumed deceased. If an individual is incorrectly identified as deceased and provides the SSA with supporting documentation, the SSA may notify certain agencies that have access to the master file, including Treasury and federal or state agencies that provide or disburse federally funded benefits.

anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.summary:
The Medication Access and Training Expansion Improvement Act (MATE Improvement Act) amends Section 303 of the Controlled Substances Act (21 U.S.C. 823) to clarify and expand the list of organizations and educational programs that can satisfy the training requirements for practitioners who prescribe controlled substances.

Existing law requires certain prescribers of controlled substances to complete training, and it specifies which professional organizations and accredited schools may provide qualifying training. This bill broadens those provisions in several ways:

- It adds the American Academy of Family Physicians, the American Podiatric Medical Association, the Academy of General Dentistry, and the American Optometric Association to the list of organizations whose training programs can count toward the requirement, and adds the Council on Podiatric Medical Education as a recognized accrediting body.
- It adds podiatric medicine to the categories of medical training (alongside osteopathic medicine and dental surgery) and references a podiatric medicine curriculum.
- For another category of qualifying training, it adds the American Pharmacists Association, the Accreditation Council on Pharmacy Education, the American Psychiatric Nurses Association, the American Academy of Nursing, and the American Academy of Family Physicians as recognized organizations.
- It adds accredited schools of pharmacy in the United States to the list of institutions whose curricula can satisfy the training requirement.

The bill also makes technical changes, including redesignating a duplicated subsection (the second subsection "(l)" becomes subsection "(m)").

The amendments are given retroactive effect: they take effect as if enacted on December 29, 2022, the date the underlying training requirement was originally established.

The bill was introduced in the Senate on March 11, 2025, by Mr. Bennet and Ms. Collins, and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

expert.summary:
The MATE Improvement Act (S. 946, 119th Congress) amends Section 303 of the Controlled Substances Act (21 U.S.C. 823) to clarify and expand the roster of organizations and professional programs recognized for purposes of the training requirement applicable to prescribers of controlled substances—the training obligation added by the Medication Access and Training Expansion (MATE) Act enacted as part of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023.

As a threshold technical correction, Section 2(a)(1) redesignates the second of two subsections erroneously both designated as subsection (l) as subsection (m), resolving a duplicate-designation drafting defect.

Section 2(a)(2) then amends the redesignated subsection (m)(1) in two respects:

For subparagraph (A) (governing the training-provider recognition and curriculum provisions for physicians and dentists), the bill: (i) in clause (iv)(I), adds the American Academy of Family Physicians, the American Podiatric Medical Association, the Academy of General Dentistry, the American Optometric Association, and the Council on Podiatric Medical Education to the list of organizations whose training satisfies the requirement, with conforming punctuation changes; (ii) in clause (iv)(III), adds the American Academy of Family Physicians; and (iii) in clause (v), adds "podiatric medicine" to the enumerated professional schools and adds a "podiatric medicine curriculum" to the recognized curricula, extending curriculum-based satisfaction of the requirement to podiatric medical education.

For subparagraph (B) (governing recognition for pharmacists and certain nursing prescribers), the bill: (i) in clause (i), adds the American Pharmacists Association, the Accreditation Council on Pharmacy Education, the American Psychiatric Nurses Association, the American Academy of Nursing, and the American Academy of Family Physicians to the recognized organizations; and (ii) in clause (ii), adds an accredited school of pharmacy to the accredited institutions whose curriculum satisfies the requirement.

Section 2(b) sets a retroactive effective date, providing that the amendments "shall take effect as if enacted on December 29, 2022"—the enactment date of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023, which contained the underlying MATE Act training provisions—so that the expanded recognition operates from the inception of the training requirement.

The bill contains no authorization of appropriations, no appropriation, and no sunset provision. Its operation is confined to conforming and expanding statutory text; it does not alter the substantive scope or duration of the eight-hour training requirement itself, only the set of qualifying providers, organizations, and educational curricula.

Its primary purpose is to clarify and expand the types of professional training and educational programs that may satisfy existing federal training requirements related to substance use disorder treatment and controlled substance prescribing.

The bill first corrects a numbering issue in section 303 of the Controlled Substances Act by redesignating the second subsection labeled “(l)” as subsection “(m).” It then amends that subsection to add several professional organizations and accrediting bodies to the lists connected with qualifying training. These include the American Academy of Family Physicians, the American Podiatric Medical Association, the Academy of General Dentistry, the American Optometric Association, and the Council on Podiatric Medical Education. It also adds the American Academy of Family Physicians in another provision relating to qualifying training.

The bill expands qualifying educational pathways by adding podiatric medicine to provisions that already refer to allopathic medicine, osteopathic medicine, dental surgery, and dental medicine, and by including dental or podiatric medicine curricula where the law refers to relevant medical or dental curricula.

For other categories of practitioners, the bill adds the American Pharmacists Association, the Accreditation Council on Pharmacy Education, the American Psychiatric Nurses Association, the American Academy of Nursing, and the American Academy of Family Physicians to the listed organizations associated with qualifying training or accreditation. It also adds accredited schools of pharmacy to the educational institutions that may satisfy the applicable training-related requirement.

These amendments are retroactive: they take effect as if they had been enacted on December 29, 2022.

Section 2(a) first corrects the codification of section 303 by redesignating the second subsection designated as subsection (l) as subsection (m). It then amends section 303(m)(1), as redesignated, which contains the required training provisions for covered practitioners seeking or maintaining registration to dispense controlled substances.

In section 303(m)(1)(A)(iv)(I), the bill adds the American Academy of Family Physicians, the American Podiatric Medical Association, the Academy of General Dentistry, and the American Optometric Association to the list of organizations whose training may qualify, and adds the Council on Podiatric Medical Education to the list of accrediting or approving bodies referenced in that clause. It also makes conforming punctuation changes. In section 303(m)(1)(A)(iv)(III), it adds the American Academy of Family Physicians to the referenced organizations. In section 303(m)(1)(A)(v), the bill expands the relevant professional education pathway by adding “podiatric medicine” to the enumerated degree programs and by referring to “dental or podiatric medicine curriculum” rather than only “dental medicine curriculum.”

Section 2(a) also amends section 303(m)(1)(B). In clause (i), it adds the American Pharmacists Association, the Accreditation Council on Pharmacy Education, the American Psychiatric Nurses Association, the American Academy of Nursing, and the American Academy of Family Physicians to the listed organizations, and separately adds the American Academy of Family Physicians to the list preceding the Accreditation Council reference. In clause (ii), it revises the school-based formulation to include “an accredited school” and expressly adds “an accredited school of pharmacy” in the United States.

Section 2(a)(1) of the bill executes a technical amendment by redesignating the second subsection designated as subsection (l) of 21 U.S.C. 823 as subsection (m). Section 2(a)(2) amends the newly redesignated subsection (m)(1), which governs the training requirements for practitioners.

Furthermore, Section 2(a)(2)(A)(ii) amends 21 U.S.C. 823(m)(1)(A)(v) to permit practitioners to satisfy the training requirement by graduating in good standing from an accredited school of podiatric medicine, or a podiatric medicine curriculum, within five years of their registration application.

crs_reference.summary:
Medication Access and Training Expansion Improvement Act or the MATE Improvement Act
This bill expands the types of organizations that may provide required training for practitioners registering with the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) to dispense (i.e., prescribe or administer) certain controlled substances.
Current law requires health care practitioners to register with the DEA and complete a one-time training on substance use disorders from specified entities in order to dispense schedule II-V controlled substances. Practitioners who graduated within the last five years from specified types of schools and whose curriculum included similar training on substance use disorders are exempt from having to receive this additional training.
The bill adds several organizations (e.g., the American Academy of Family Physicians) to the list of entities that may provide the required one-time training for physicians or other practitioners. It also expands the types of practitioners who are exempt from this training requirement to include those who graduated from schools of podiatric medicine or schools of pharmacy within the last five years and received similar training as part of their curriculums.
The bill applies retroactively, taking effect as if enacted on December 29, 2022.

The "Improving Access to Addiction Medicine Providers Act" (S. 1036) is a bill introduced in the U.S. Senate that would amend Section 597 of the Public Health Service Act, which governs the Minority Fellowship Program.

The bill makes two specific changes to existing law. First, in the provision describing the program's purpose, it inserts the word "diagnosis" into the list of activities for which the program is relevant. Second, it adds "addiction medicine" to the list of professional fields—which already includes psychiatry—for which fellowships under the Minority Fellowship Program may be awarded.

The overall effect of these amendments is to authorize fellowships under the Minority Fellowship Program to be used for training professionals in the addiction medicine field.

The bill does not specify a particular effective date, and it contains no separate exceptions or conditions beyond the textual amendments described. It was introduced on March 13, 2025, by Senators Cornyn and Luján and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

expert.summary:
The Improving Access to Addiction Medicine Providers Act (S. 1036, 119th Congress) is a short amendatory bill directed at expanding the scope of the Minority Fellowship Program authorized under Section 597 of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. 290ll).

Section 1 establishes the short title. Section 2 makes two conforming textual amendments to Section 597:

First, in subsection (a)(1), the bill inserts the word "diagnosis," after the phrase "related to," thereby broadening the enumerated activities or competencies for which fellowship-supported training may be directed to include diagnosis.

Second, in subsection (b), which enumerates the disciplines eligible for fellowship support, the bill inserts "addiction medicine," after "psychiatry," adding addiction medicine to the list of professional fields for which fellowships may be awarded under the program.

The operative mechanism is limited to these insertions into existing statutory text; the bill creates no new program, standalone authority, or appropriation. It does not amend the program's funding authorization, alter administration by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, modify eligibility criteria beyond adding the specified discipline, or affect the underlying grant-making structure. No new authorization of appropriations is provided, and no separate appropriation is made—the amendments operate within the pre-existing statutory framework of Section 597.

The bill contains no severability clause, no sunset provision, no delayed effective date, and no conditions precedent. Absent a specified effective date, the amendments take effect upon enactment. As introduced on March 13, 2025, by Senators Cornyn and Luján, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

The "Halting the Epidemic of Addiction and Loss Act of 2025" (S. 2336) directs the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to ensure that references to opioid overdose reversal drugs in certain federal grant programs are not limited to naloxone specifically, but instead encompass all approved overdose reversal medications.

The bill requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to ensure that, as appropriate, whenever HHS issues a regulation or guidance for any grant program addressing opioid misuse and use disorders, any reference to an opioid overdose reversal drug (such as a reference to naloxone) is inclusive of any opioid overdose reversal drug approved under section 505 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act for emergency treatment of a known or suspected opioid overdose.

The bill also addresses existing references in HHS regulations and guidance. Within one year of enactment, the Secretary must update all qualifying references to be inclusive of any opioid overdose reversal drug approved or otherwise authorized for use by the Food and Drug Administration. This updating requirement applies to references to overdose reversal drugs that were issued before the date of enactment and that appear in two specific grant programs: (1) the grant program for State and Tribal response to opioid use disorders under section 1003 of the 21st Century Cures Act (commonly known as "State Opioid Response Grants" and "Tribal Opioid Response Grants"); and (2) the grant program for priority substance use disorder prevention needs of regional and national significance under section 516 of the Public Health Service Act.

The bill was introduced in the Senate on July 17, 2025, by Senators Cornyn and Hassan, and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

The government helps pay for programs that fight opioid problems. This money is called a "grant." When the government writes rules for these programs, it often names naloxone as the reversal medicine.

This bill says the government should not only name naloxone. It should include any reversal medicine that has been approved by the FDA (the group that decides which medicines are safe to use) for treating an opioid overdose.

Here is what would change if this becomes law:
- When the government writes new rules or advice for these opioid programs, it must include all approved reversal medicines, not just naloxone.
- Within one year, the government must also update its old rules and advice to include all approved reversal medicines.

This applies to two money programs: one that helps states and Native American tribes deal with opioid problems, and one for important drug-prevention needs.

The bill was introduced in the Senate on July 17, 2025.

expert.summary:
The bill, titled the "Halting the Epidemic of Addiction and Loss Act of 2025" (S. 2336, 119th Congress), directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to ensure that references to opioid overdose reversal agents in specified HHS grant programs are not limited to naloxone. The bill's operative mechanism is a mandate to construe or update regulatory and guidance references to encompass all FDA-approved opioid overdose reversal drugs.

Section 2(a) imposes a prospective, ongoing obligation: whenever the Department issues a regulation or guidance for any grant program addressing opioid misuse and use disorders, the Secretary shall ensure, "as appropriate," that any reference to an opioid overdose reversal drug (such as naloxone) is inclusive of any opioid overdose reversal drug approved under section 505 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 U.S.C. 355) for emergency treatment of a known or suspected opioid overdose. The "as appropriate" qualifier and the FDCA section 505 approval standard condition the scope of this general rule.

Section 2(b) addresses existing references retrospectively. Under paragraph (1), not later than one year after the date of enactment, the Secretary shall update all covered references to be inclusive of any opioid overdose reversal drug "approved or otherwise authorized for use" by the FDA. Notably, this update provision employs a broader authorization standard ("approved or otherwise authorized") than the section 505 approval standard used in subsection (a).

Paragraph (2) delimits the covered references to those appearing in any HHS regulation or guidance that (A) was issued before the date of enactment and (B) is included in one of two specified grant programs: (i) the State and Tribal response to opioid use disorders grant program under section 1003 of the 21st Century Cures Act (42 U.S.C. 290ee-3a) (the State Opioid Response Grants and Tribal Opioid Response Grants); or (ii) the grant program for priority substance use disorder prevention needs of regional and national significance under section 516 of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. 290bb-22).

The bill amends no existing statutory text directly, contains no repeals or sunset provisions, and includes no authorization or appropriation of funds. Its sole enforceable deadline is the one-year update requirement in subsection (b)(1); the subsection (a) obligation applies on an ongoing basis upon enactment. The bill has been read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

This bill, the “Halting the Epidemic of Addiction and Loss Act of 2025,” directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to ensure that references to opioid overdose reversal agents in certain departmental grant programs are not limited to naloxone but are inclusive of other FDA-approved or authorized drugs.

Section 2(a) imposes a prospective requirement: whenever the Department of Health and Human Services issues a regulation or guidance for any grant program addressing opioid misuse and use disorders, the Secretary shall ensure, as appropriate, that any reference to an opioid overdose reversal drug (such as naloxone) is inclusive of any opioid overdose reversal drug approved under section 505 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 U.S.C. 355) for emergency treatment of a known or suspected opioid overdose.

Section 2(b) addresses existing references. Not later than one year after enactment, the Secretary must update all references to an opioid overdose reversal drug (such as naloxone) in any HHS regulation or guidance issued before enactment that is part of two specified grant programs: (1) the State and Tribal response to opioid use disorders grant program under section 1003 of the 21st Century Cures Act (42 U.S.C. 290ee-3a), commonly known as State Opioid Response Grants and Tribal Opioid Response Grants; and (2) the grant program for priority substance use disorder prevention needs of regional and national significance under section 516 of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. 290bb-22). For these existing references, the update must make them inclusive of any opioid overdose reversal drug that has been approved or otherwise authorized for use by the Food and Drug Administration—a broader category than the prospective requirement’s reference to section 505 approval alone.

The bill contains no appropriations, authorizations of appropriations, or sunset provisions. It establishes a mandatory duty for the Secretary, qualified by the phrase “as appropriate” in the prospective provision, and sets a one-year deadline for the retrospective update.

The Safe Response Act (S. 2532), introduced July 30, 2025, is a single-purpose reauthorization bill amending Section 546 of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. 290ee-1), which authorizes the first responder training program administered under that Act. The bill effects both substantive scope changes and a reauthorization of appropriations.

The operative mechanism is a series of textual amendments to Section 546. First, in subsection (a), the bill conforms capitalization by striking "tribes and tribal" and inserting "Tribes and Tribal."

Second, the bill expands the class of covered drugs and devices. Throughout subsections (a), (c), (d), and (f), it strikes "approved or cleared" and inserts "approved, cleared, or otherwise legally marketed"—broadening the categories of products (e.g., overdose-reversal drugs and devices) that fall within the program's scope to include those legally marketed outside formal approval or clearance pathways.

Third, the bill removes the program's exclusive focus on opioids. It strikes the word "opioid" wherever it appears in subsections (a), (c), and (d), and in subsection (f)(1). In subsection (f)(2), it strikes "opioid and heroin" and inserts "opioid, heroin, and other drug," and strikes "opioid overdose" in favor of the broader "overdose." In subsection (f)(3), it strikes "opioid and heroin." The cumulative effect is to extend the training program's authorized activities—including training on administration of overdose-reversal products and on the treatment and recognition of overdoses—to drug overdoses generally rather than limiting them to opioid- and heroin-related overdoses.

Fourth, the bill reauthorizes the program's funding. In subsection (h), it strikes the prior authorization of "$36,000,000 for each of fiscal years 2019 through 2023" and inserts "$57,000,000 for each of fiscal years 2026 through 2030." This is an authorization of appropriations, not an appropriation; it establishes a ceiling of $57,000,000 per fiscal year over the FY2026–FY2030 period and does not itself provide budget authority.

The bill contains no separate effective-date provision, severability clause, or conditions precedent; the amendments take effect upon enactment. No new deadlines or reporting requirements are added beyond those already contained in existing Section 546. The bill was referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.summary:
The Bankruptcy Administration Improvement Act of 2025 amends titles 11 and 28 of the U.S. Code to increase compensation for chapter 7 bankruptcy trustees, adjust certain bankruptcy fees, and extend the terms of some temporary bankruptcy judgeships. The bill states that the bankruptcy system is intended to be self-funding at no cost to taxpayers, and notes that trustee compensation has not increased since 1994.

Trustee Compensation: The bill amends Section 330 of title 11 to raise one component of a trustee's per-case compensation from $45 to $105 (with the existing $15 component, this brings total compensation to $120 per case) and repeals subsection 330(e). It directs how the remainder of fees collected under section 1930(a)(1)(A) are deposited, allocating $63.51 to a Treasury special fund, $25.00 to a fund under the Deficit Reduction Act of 2005, and $51.49 to the United States Trustee System Fund. Corresponding changes are made to Section 589a of title 28.

Bankruptcy Fees: The bill modifies quarterly fees under Section 1930(a)(6)(B), extending a "5-year" reference to "10-year," and revising fee calculation formulas (including changing a 0.8 figure to 0.9). It extends related deposit provisions from 2026 to 2031 and specifies how fees are deposited for fiscal years 2026 through 2031, including depositing $5,400,000 annually into the Treasury's general fund.

Temporary Judgeships: The bill amends the Bankruptcy Administration Improvement Act of 2020 and the Bankruptcy Judgeship Act of 2017 to extend the terms of specified temporary bankruptcy judge offices from 5 years to 10 years.

The bill states it will not alter the chapter 7 filing fee and will not affect courts' authority to waive filing fees for indigent individuals.

Effective Dates: The amendments generally take effect on the first calendar quarter beginning on or after enactment. The trustee compensation changes apply to cases commenced on or after the first October 1 after enactment. The fee changes apply to cases pending or commenced, and disbursements made, on or after the first applicable quarter. The Act was approved February 6, 2025.

expert.summary:
The Bankruptcy Administration Improvement Act of 2025 (Pub. L. 119-76; S. 3424), enacted February 6, 2025, amends titles 11 and 28 of the U.S. Code to (1) increase chapter 7 trustee compensation, (2) modify and reallocate bankruptcy fees, and (3) extend the terms of certain temporary bankruptcy judgeships.

**Trustee compensation (Section 3).** Section 3(a) amends 11 U.S.C. § 330(b)(1) by striking "$45" and inserting "$105," raising the fixed per-case trustee payment (which, combined with the unchanged $15 under § 330(b)(2), yields $120 per case per the findings). It repeals § 330(e). Section 3(b) directs, notwithstanding any other law, that the remainder of fees collected under 28 U.S.C. § 1930(a)(1)(A) after trustee compensation be deposited as follows: $63.51 to the § 1931 special fund; $25.00 to the special fund under section 10101(b) of the Deficit Reduction Act of 2005; and $51.49 to the United States Trustee System Fund (28 U.S.C. § 589a). Section 3(c) conformingly amends § 589a(b)(1)(A), substituting a fixed "$51.49 of the fees collected in each case" for "40.46 percent," and restructures the deposit-priority provisions of § 589a(f)(1) by striking subparagraphs (B) and (C), redesignating (D) as (B), and changing "Fourth" to "Second."

**Bankruptcy fees (Section 4).** Section 4(a) amends the chapter 11 quarterly-fee provision at 28 U.S.C. § 1930(a)(6)(B): extending the applicable period in clause (i) from "5-year" to "10-year," and in clause (ii) revising the fee formula to "the greater of" 0.4 percent "or" (rather than "and") a rate raised in subclause (II) from 0.8 to 0.9 percent. Section 4(b) extends deposit-period references in § 589a(f) from "2026" to "2031." Section 4(c) provides that, for fiscal years 2026 through 2031, notwithstanding § 589a(b), § 1930(a)(6) fees be deposited per § 589a(f), except that $5,400,000 annually be deposited in the general fund of the Treasury.

**Temporary judgeships (Section 5).** Section 5(a) amends Section 4 of the Bankruptcy Administration Improvement Act of 2020 (28 U.S.C. § 152 note) by striking "5 years" and inserting "10 years" throughout numerous subsections. Section 5(b) makes the same extension to Section 1003(b)(2)(A) of the Bankruptcy Judgeship Act of 2017.

**Effective dates (Section 6).** Amendments generally take effect on the first calendar quarter beginning on or after enactment. Exceptions: Section 3 applies to chapter 7 cases (and chapter 11/12/13 cases converted to chapter 7) commenced on or after the first October 1 after enactment; Section 4 applies to chapter 11 cases commenced or pending as of the first post-enactment quarter and to quarterly fees for disbursements in quarters beginning on or after enactment.

The findings state the Act does not alter chapter 7 filing fees or affect courts' authority to waive fees for indigent individuals.
