expert.summary:
The **Bankruptcy Administration Improvement Act of 2025** (Pub. L. 119-76) amends Titles 11 and 28 of the United States Code to restructure chapter 7 trustee compensation, adjust chapter 11 quarterly fees, and extend temporary bankruptcy judgeships.

### Trustee Compensation and Fund Allocation
Section 3(a) amends 11 U.S.C. § 330(b)(1) to increase the statutory compensation paid to chapter 7 trustees from $45 to $105 per case, and repeals 11 U.S.C. § 330(e). 

Section 3(b) directs that the remainder of the filing fees collected under 28 U.S.C. § 1930(a)(1)(A), after paying the § 330(b)(1) trustee compensation, be deposited as follows:
*   $63.51 into the Treasury special fund established under 28 U.S.C. § 1931;
*   $25.00 into the special fund established under section 10101(b) of the Deficit Reduction Act of 2005 (28 U.S.C. § 1931 note); and
*   $51.49 into the United States Trustee System Fund established under 28 U.S.C. § 589a.

Section 3(c) amends 28 U.S.C. § 589a(b)(1)(A) by replacing the allocation of "40.46 percent of the fees collected" with a flat "$51.49 of the fees collected in each case." It also amends 28 U.S.C. § 589a(f)(1) by striking subparagraphs (B) and (C), redesignating subparagraph (D) as (B), and changing a priority reference from "Fourth" to "Second."

### Bankruptcy Fees and Deposits
Section 4(a) amends 28 U.S.C. § 1930(a)(6)(B) to extend the application of certain chapter 11 quarterly fees from a 5-year period to a 10-year period. It modifies the fee calculation formula under clause (ii) to apply "the greater of" 0.4 percent of disbursements or a rate of 0.9 percent (increased from 0.8 percent) if the United States Trustee System Fund balance exceeds $200,000,000.

Section 4(b) amends 28 U.S.C. § 589a(f) to extend the deposit period for these fees from 2026 to 2031. Section 4(c) establishes a statutory carve-out for fiscal years 2026 through 2031, directing that fees collected under 28 U.S.C. § 1930(a)(6) be deposited pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 589a(f), except that $5,400,000 annually must be deposited into the general fund of the Treasury.

### Extension of Temporary Bankruptcy Judgeships
Section 5 extends the terms of specified temporary bankruptcy judgeships from 5 years to 10 years by amending:
*   Section 4 of the Bankruptcy Administration Improvement Act of 2020 (28 U.S.C. § 152 note) across subsections (a) through (f); and
*   Section 1003(b)(2)(A) of the Bankruptcy Judgeship Act of 2017 (28 U.S.C. § 152 note).

### Effective Dates and Applicability
Under Section 6, the Act generally takes effect on the first day of the first calendar quarter occurring on or after enactment (February 6, 2026). However, specific exceptions apply:
*   **Trustee Compensation (Section 3):** Applies to cases commenced under chapter 7, or converted to chapter 7 from chapters 11, 12, or 13, on or after the first October 1 occurring after enactment.
*   **Bankruptcy Fees (Section 4):** Applies to cases commenced or pending under chapter 11 on the first day of the first calendar quarter occurring on or after enactment, and to quarterly fees under 28 U.S.C. § 1930(a)(6) for disbursements made in any calendar quarter beginning on or after enactment.

anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.summary:
The "Florida Freeze Disaster Assistance Act" (S. 4663) appropriates funds for the Secretary of Agriculture to provide disaster relief to agricultural producers affected by freezing or cold weather conditions.

The bill appropriates $3,500,000,000 from the Treasury for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2027, as an additional amount under "Agricultural Programs—Office of the Secretary." These funds would remain available until expended.

The Secretary of Agriculture would use the money to provide assistance in the form of block grants to States to compensate for losses of revenue, quality, or production of crops (including crops prevented from being planted), trees, bushes, and vines that result from a freeze or cold weather condition. The assistance must include compensation to producers for losses of multi-year crops.

The bill places several conditions on the funds. They may be used exclusively for losses occurring in counties that received a disaster designation for freeze and related cold weather conditions issued by the Secretary on March 4, 2026. The funds become available only upon the request of a State department of agriculture or other appropriate State agency, as determined by the Secretary.

The bill requires reporting: no later than 120 days after enactment, and for each fiscal quarter thereafter until the funds are fully expended, the Secretary must submit reports to the Appropriations Committees of the House and Senate describing how the assistance is being implemented.

Finally, the appropriated amount is designated by Congress as an emergency requirement under section 251(b)(2)(A)(i) of the Balanced Budget and Emergency Deficit Control Act of 1985.

The bill was introduced in the Senate on June 2, 2026, by Mr. Scott of Florida and Mrs. Moody, and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.

expert.summary:
The Florida Freeze Disaster Assistance Act (S. 4663, 119th Congress) is a single-purpose appropriations measure directing the Secretary of Agriculture to provide block grants to States for agricultural revenue losses attributable to freeze or cold weather conditions.

Section 1 supplies the short title. Section 2 constitutes the operative provision, appropriating $3,500,000,000 out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2027, as an additional amount under the "Agricultural Programs—Office of the Secretary" account. The appropriation is designated to remain available until expended (no-year funds), and is provided directly (an appropriation, not merely an authorization).

The funds are to be used by the Secretary to provide assistance in the form of block grants to States for losses of revenue, quality, or production of crops (including crops prevented from planting), trees, bushes, and vines, resulting from a freeze or cold weather condition.

The section imposes several conditions and provisos:

- The assistance "shall include" compensation to producers for losses of multi-year crops (a mandatory inclusion within the covered loss categories).
- Funds are made available "exclusively" for losses occurring in counties that received a disaster designation for freeze and related cold weather conditions issued by the Secretary on March 4, 2026. This date-specific and county-specific designation operates as a condition precedent limiting eligibility.
- Funds are made available upon the request of a State department of agriculture or other appropriate State agency, as determined by the Secretary, establishing a State-request mechanism as a condition of disbursement.
- A reporting requirement obligates the Secretary, not later than 120 days after the date of enactment and for each fiscal quarter thereafter until the amounts are expended, to submit reports to the House and Senate Committees on Appropriations describing implementation.

Finally, the appropriated amount is designated by Congress as an emergency requirement pursuant to section 251(b)(2)(A)(i) of the Balanced Budget and Emergency Deficit Control Act of 1985 (2 U.S.C. 901(b)(2)(A)(i)), a designation that has the effect of exempting the amount from applicable discretionary spending limits.

The bill contains no separate effective-date provision (thus taking effect upon enactment), no amendment to existing U.S. Code provisions, no sunset apart from the practical exhaustion of the no-year appropriation, and no separate authorization of appropriations distinct from the direct appropriation itself. The bill was introduced June 2, 2026, by Mr. Scott of Florida (for himself and Mrs. Moody) and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.

The Declaration of Independence Reaffirmation Act of 2026 (S. 4828) is a Senate-passed bill whose primary purpose is to formally reaffirm the Declaration of Independence as an Organic Law of the United States, in commemoration of the 250th anniversary of American independence.

The bill begins with congressional findings reviewing the history and significance of the Declaration of Independence. These findings note that the Declaration was adopted on July 4, 1776, that it is recognized among the Organic Laws of the United States, and that it declares principles such as human equality, unalienable rights endowed by a Creator, and government deriving its just powers from the consent of the governed. The findings also reference the Northwest Ordinance (adopted in 1787 and reenacted in 1789), assert that Congress has authority to recognize and carry forward foundational laws, and describe the relationship between the Declaration and the Constitution in establishing a political order in which the people are sovereign.

The bill's main operative provision states that Congress reaffirms and re-adopts the Declaration of Independence as an Organic Law of the United States and as the "enduring charter of American independence, national sovereignty, natural rights, equal citizenship, and government by consent."

The bill then sets forth the complete text of the Declaration of Independence, presented in commemoration of the 250th anniversary of American independence.

The bill does not create new programs, alter existing statutory rights or obligations, appropriate funds, or impose any deadlines or enforcement mechanisms. Its provisions are declaratory and commemorative in nature. The bill includes a short title but specifies no effective date. As reflected in the text, the Senate read the bill twice, considered it, read it a third time, and passed it on June 18, 2026.

S. 4828, the "Declaration of Independence Reaffirmation Act of 2026," is a Senate-passed bill (considered and passed June 18, 2026) whose sole operative purpose is to reaffirm and re-adopt the Declaration of Independence as an Organic Law of the United States. The bill is declaratory and commemorative in character; it creates no new statutory authority, appropriates no funds, and amends no provision of the U.S. Code or any named prior Act.

Section 1 provides the short title.

Section 2 sets forth ten congressional findings, including that the Continental Congress adopted the Declaration on July 4, 1776; that the Declaration is recognized among the Organic Laws of the United States; that the Northwest Ordinance was adopted by the Congress of the Confederation in 1787 and reenacted by the First Congress in 1789 to retain effect under the Constitution; that Congress has authority to recognize, reaffirm, and carry forward the foundational laws and principles of the American political order; and that the 250th anniversary of American independence occasions reaffirmation of the Declaration as the charter of American sovereignty, natural rights, equal citizenship, and government by consent. The findings further characterize the Declaration and Constitution as together establishing a political order in which the people are sovereign, and describe Americans as "one people" with the right to self-government, national independence, and the securing of their citizens' rights.

Section 3 is the operative provision: "Congress reaffirms and re-adopts the Declaration of Independence as an Organic Law of the United States and as the enduring charter of American independence, national sovereignty, natural rights, equal citizenship, and government by consent." The provision effects a reaffirmation and re-adoption but prescribes no implementing mechanism, enforcement authority, rulemaking directive, or private right of action.

Section 4, expressly framed as commemorating the 250th anniversary of American independence, sets forth verbatim the full text of the Declaration of Independence, from the preamble through the enumerated grievances and the concluding declaration of independence.

The bill contains no effective-date provision, no deadlines, no sunset, no conditions precedent, and no authorization or appropriation of funds. Because it operates solely through findings, a reaffirmation clause, and the recitation of the Declaration's text, its legal effect is confined to the statutory reaffirmation set out in Section 3.

This joint resolution, enacted as Public Law 119-3, uses Congress's authority under the Congressional Review Act (chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code) to overturn a federal regulation.

Specifically, Congress disapproves the rule issued by the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management titled "Protection of Marine Archaeological Resources," which was published in the Federal Register on September 3, 2024 (89 Fed. Reg. 71160). Under the resolution, this rule "shall have no force or effect," meaning the regulation is nullified and cannot be implemented or enforced.

The Congressional Review Act provides a mechanism for Congress to review and reject rules issued by federal agencies. When a disapproval resolution such as this one is enacted, the targeted rule is treated as though it had never taken effect.

The resolution passed the Senate on February 25, 2025, passed the House on March 6, 2025, and was approved on March 14, 2025.

expert.summary:
This joint resolution, enacted as Public Law 119-3, exercises Congress's authority under the Congressional Review Act (chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code) to disapprove a final rule promulgated by an executive agency.

The resolution's sole operative provision states that Congress disapproves the rule submitted by the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM) relating to "Protection of Marine Archaeological Resources," published at 89 Fed. Reg. 71160 (September 3, 2024), and provides that "such rule shall have no force or effect."

The mechanism is that of 5 U.S.C. § 801(b)(1), under which a rule shall not take effect (or continue in effect) if Congress enacts a joint resolution of disapproval. By operation of the Congressional Review Act, the disapproved rule is treated as though it had never taken effect. Additionally, under 5 U.S.C. § 801(b)(2), the agency is barred from reissuing the rule in substantially the same form, or issuing a new rule that is substantially the same as the disapproved rule, unless the reissued or new rule is specifically authorized by a law enacted after the date of the joint resolution's enactment.

The resolution originated as S.J. Res. 11 in the 119th Congress. It was considered and passed by the Senate on February 25, 2025, and considered and passed by the House on March 6, 2025. It was approved (signed into law) on March 14, 2025.

The resolution contains no separate effective-date provision, no authorization of appropriations, and no amendment to any provision of the United States Code; its effect is confined to nullifying the identified BOEM rule and triggering the reissuance limitation attendant to Congressional Review Act disapprovals. The text specifies no conditions precedent, exceptions, or delegated implementing authority beyond the disapproval itself.

This joint resolution, enacted as Public Law 119-47, exercises Congress's disapproval authority under the Congressional Review Act (CRA), codified at chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code (5 U.S.C. §§ 801 et seq.), to nullify an agency action of the Bureau of Land Management (BLM).

The resolution's sole operative provision disapproves the BLM action designated "National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska Integrated Activity Plan Record of Decision," issued April 25, 2022, as a record of decision. Pursuant to the standard CRA mechanism under 5 U.S.C. § 801(b)(1), the resolution provides that the disapproved rule "shall have no force or effect." By operation of 5 U.S.C. § 801(b)(2), a rule disapproved by enacted joint resolution may not be reissued in substantially the same form, nor may a new rule that is substantially the same be issued, absent subsequent statutory authorization.

A notable feature of this resolution is its treatment of the underlying agency action as a "rule" subject to CRA review. The resolution expressly references a Government Accountability Office letter of opinion dated July 24, 2025, printed in the Congressional Record at pages S4768–S4770 (July 28, 2025), which concluded that the record of decision constitutes a "rule" within the meaning of the CRA. This GAO determination is the predicate for CRA applicability, as records of decision are not ordinarily processed as rules submitted under 5 U.S.C. § 801(a)(1); the GAO opinion effectively established the reviewability threshold and, under established CRA practice, can reset the periods for congressional action.

The resolution contains no amendments to the United States Code, no authorizations of appropriations, no appropriations, and no sunset provisions. Its legal effect is limited to the invalidation of the identified record of decision and the attendant statutory bar on substantially similar future action.

The measure was enacted through the CRA's expedited procedures. Legislative history reflects that S.J. Res. 80 was considered and passed by the Senate on October 30, 2025, and considered and passed by the House on November 18, 2025. It was approved December 5, 2025. The effective date is the date of enactment; the resolution takes effect upon approval, rendering the disapproved record of decision without force or effect as of that date.

The resolution opens with findings asserting that Congress holds the sole constitutional power to declare war, that the President has a constitutional responsibility to defend the United States and its people from attack, and that Congress has neither declared war on Iran nor enacted a specific statutory authorization for military force against Iran. It states that using military force within or against Iran constitutes introducing U.S. Armed Forces into hostilities under Section 4(a) of the War Powers Resolution.

The operative provision invokes Section 1013 of the Department of State Authorization Act for Fiscal Years 1984 and 1985 and the expedited procedures of Section 601(b) of the International Security Assistance and Arms Export Control Act of 1976. Under these authorities, Congress directs the President to remove U.S. Armed Forces from hostilities within or against Iran unless such action is explicitly authorized by a declaration of war or a specific authorization for the use of military force.

The resolution includes a rule of construction clarifying that it does not prevent the United States from:
- defending against an attack on the United States or its personnel or facilities in other nations;
- collecting, analyzing, or sharing intelligence—including with partner countries attacked by Iran since February 28, 2026, and other nations and international organizations—related to defense from threats from Iran or its proxies; or
- assisting partner countries attacked by Iran since February 28, 2026, and other nations, either by intercepting retaliatory attacks on their territory by Iran or its proxies, or by providing defensive materiel support for such measures.

The resolution does not specify a deadline for the removal of forces. It was referred to the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations.

S.J. Res. 163, introduced by Senator Merkley on April 13, 2026, is a privileged joint resolution invoking Congress's war powers to direct the removal of United States Armed Forces from unauthorized hostilities within or against the Islamic Republic of Iran.

Section 1 sets forth congressional findings, including that Congress holds the sole power to declare war under Article I, Section 8, Clause 11; that Congress has neither declared war on Iran nor enacted a specific statutory authorization for the use of military force within or against Iran; and that such use of force constitutes the introduction of Armed Forces into hostilities within the meaning of section 4(a) of the War Powers Resolution (50 U.S.C. 1543(a)). The findings further characterize the resolution as one qualifying for expedited (privileged) floor consideration pursuant to section 1013 of the Department of State Authorization Act, Fiscal Years 1984 and 1985 (50 U.S.C. 1546a), which incorporates the expedited procedures of section 601(b) of the International Security Assistance and Arms Export Control Act of 1976 (Pub. L. 94-329).

Section 2(a) is the operative directive. Pursuant to 50 U.S.C. 1546a and section 601(b) of the 1976 Act, Congress directs the President to remove the Armed Forces from hostilities within or against Iran unless such hostilities are explicitly authorized by a declaration of war or a specific authorization for use of military force. The provision does not amend the U.S. Code; it operates as a stand-alone congressional directive under the War Powers framework and does not specify a removal deadline within its own text (the underlying statutory procedures supply the timing and expedited-consideration mechanism).

Section 2(b) supplies a rule of construction providing that nothing in the section may be construed to prevent the United States from: (1) defending against an attack on the United States or its personnel or facilities in other nations; (2) collecting, analyzing, or sharing intelligence—including with partner countries attacked by Iran since February 28, 2026, and other nations and international organizations—related to defense from threats from Iran or its proxies; or (3) assisting partner countries attacked by Iran since February 28, 2026, and other nations by intercepting retaliatory attacks on their territory by Iran or its proxies, or by providing defensive materiel support for such defensive measures.

expert.summary:
S.J. Res. 180, introduced in the 119th Congress, is a joint resolution directing the President to remove United States Armed Forces from unauthorized hostilities within or against the Islamic Republic of Iran. 

Section 1 sets forth congressional findings. It asserts Congress’s sole power to declare war under Article I, Section 8, Clause 11 of the Constitution, and notes that Congress has not declared war or enacted a specific statutory authorization for the use of military force within or against Iran. The findings identify "Operation Epic Fury," initiated on February 28, 2026, as introducing U.S. Armed Forces into hostilities within the meaning of section 4(a) of the War Powers Resolution (50 U.S.C. 1543(a)). Section 1 further invokes section 1013 of the Department of State Authorization Act, Fiscal Years 1984 and 1985 (50 U.S.C. 1546a), which subjects joint resolutions requiring the removal of U.S. Armed Forces from unauthorized hostilities to the expedited legislative procedures of section 601(b) of the International Security Assistance and Arms Export Control Act of 1976 (Public Law 94-329).

Section 2(a) contains the operative mandate. Pursuant to 50 U.S.C. 1546a and in accordance with section 601(b) of Public Law 94-329, Congress directs the President to remove U.S. Armed Forces from hostilities within or against Iran. This removal mandate is subject to a condition precedent: it applies unless and until such hostilities are explicitly authorized by a congressional declaration of war or a specific authorization for the use of military force. 

Section 2(b) establishes rules of construction that exempt specific military and intelligence activities from the removal mandate. The directive may not be construed to prevent the United States from:
1. Defending against attacks on the United States, its personnel, or its facilities in other nations;
2. Collecting, analyzing, or sharing intelligence—including with partner countries attacked by Iran since February 28, 2026, other nations, and international organizations—concerning threats from Iran or its proxies;
3. Assisting partner countries attacked by Iran since February 28, 2026, and other nations, by intercepting retaliatory Iranian or proxy attacks on their territory or by providing defensive materiel support; or
4. Providing security, departure, and evacuation assistance to U.S. citizens affected by the hostilities.

The resolution does not amend the U.S. Code; it is a standalone legislative directive backed by findings that Congress has neither declared war nor enacted a specific statutory authorization for use of military force (AUMF) with respect to Iran, and that military operations including enforcement of a naval blockade trigger Section 4(a) of the War Powers Resolution (50 U.S.C. § 1543(a)).

Section 1 sets forth three findings: (1) Congress’s exclusive power to declare war under Article I, Section 8, Clause 11; (2) the President’s constitutional responsibility to defend the United States, its territories, possessions, citizens, servicemembers, and diplomats from attack; and (3) the absence of a war declaration or specific statutory AUMF for military force within or against Iran. A fourth finding states that the introduction of forces into hostilities within or against Iran, including enforcing a naval blockade, constitutes “introduction of United States Armed Forces into hostilities” under Section 4(a) of the War Powers Resolution. A fifth finding invokes Section 1013 of the Department of State Authorization Act, Fiscal Years 1984 and 1985 (50 U.S.C. § 1546a) and Section 601(b) of the International Security Assistance and Arms Export Control Act of 1976 (Public Law 94-329) to apply expedited congressional procedures.

Section 2(a) directs the President, pursuant to 50 U.S.C. § 1546a and in accordance with Public Law 94-329, to remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities within or against Iran, unless such hostilities are explicitly authorized by a declaration of war or a specific AUMF. Section 2(b) contains a rule of construction preserving the United States’ authority to (1) defend against an attack on the United States or its personnel or facilities in other nations; (2) collect, analyze, or share intelligence with partner countries attacked by Iran since February 28, 2026, and with other nations and international organizations, regarding threats from Iran or its proxies; and (3) assist such partner countries and other nations in intercepting retaliatory attacks by Iran or its proxies and in providing defensive materiel support for such defensive measures. The resolution includes no authorization of appropriations, no effective date apart from enactment, and no sunset provision. The directive operates as a mandatory withdrawal order subject to the stated exceptions.

The proposed article contains four operative sections.

Section 1 confers an affirmative individual right: it provides that every citizen of the United States of legal voting age shall have the fundamental right to vote in any public election held in the jurisdiction of the citizen's residence. The text does not define "legal voting age," "public election," or "jurisdiction."

Section 2 establishes a substantive standard of review governing infringements of the right. It bars the United States, any State, or any political subdivision within a State from denying or abridging the fundamental right to vote unless the denial or abridgment (i) furthers a compelling governmental interest and (ii) constitutes the least restrictive means of furthering that interest. This language codifies a strict-scrutiny test as the constitutional standard applicable to voting-rights restrictions.

Section 3 effects a partial repeal of an existing constitutional provision. It repeals the phrase "or other crime" from Section 2 of the Fourteenth Amendment. That clause presently permits reduction of a State's basis of congressional representation when the right to vote is denied or abridged, "except for participation in rebellion, or other crime." Write a precise, technical summary of the bill text below. Your summary should:
- State the bill's primary purpose and operative mechanism.
- Describe its major provisions with statutory precision: cite section numbers, named acts, and U.S. Code provisions the bill amends, and characterize each change (new authority, repeal, sunset, authorization, appropriation, etc.).
- Note material exceptions, conditions precedent, effective dates, deadlines, and authorization-versus-appropriation distinctions.
- Use standard legislative drafting terminology; do not simplify terms of art.
- Stay strictly neutral — no opinion, advocacy, or speculation.
- Be faithful to the text — include nothing that is not in the bill.
